sources.title: How Tabs hit $11M in 18 months: viral product design, creator networks and funnel stacking
sources.originalTitle: From Idea to $11M in 18 Months | Oliver Brocato - Tabs
sources.summary: Oliver Brocato explains how he built Tabs, a sex-chocolate brand, by designing the product to go viral on TikTok. He covers running hundreds of independent creator accounts, the one-two punch of viral video plus comment-reply retargeting, funnel upsells that double AOV, and price testing.

principles.text: Build a real brand, not a dropshipping store. Brands build LTV and equity, and the exit is where the real wealth is.
principles.quote: with a brand You're Building equity and by the way like the real wealth comes from the exit not from the cash flow

principles.text: Design the product backwards from distribution: make something that lends itself to organically going viral.
principles.quote: I kind of reverse engineered it where I was like how do I build a product that's going to go viral that lends itself to organically going viral

principles.text: Cast a wide net: hundreds of independent creator accounts, because enough daily content guarantees some hits.
principles.quote: I know that inevitably if I have enough content going out every single day one is going to hit and all I need is one to hit in order to drive serious impact in sales

principles.text: Use a one-two punch on TikTok: optimize the first video for views, then sell hard in comment-reply videos that retarget viewers for free.
principles.quote: the viral video is not what drives the majority of the sales it's the follow-up videos that drives the true conversions

principles.text: Stack upsells across the funnel (cart add-on, checkout subscription, post-purchase, thank-you page) to multiply AOV on the same traffic.
principles.quote: the person that's able to squeeze the most out of money will win long term

principles.text: Test higher prices. For a luxury, novel product, raising the price lifted conversion, because price signals quality.
principles.quote: when we increase price we saw an increase in conversion

sources.title: How Oliver Brocato built Tabs Chocolate to $11M/year with one product and a UGC content machine
sources.originalTitle: I Make $11M/Year Selling One Product
sources.summary: Oliver Brocato explains how he turned a viral-validated novelty product (sex chocolate) into an $11M/year brand with no outside funding. He covers picking a product that triggers emotion, building a brand instead of dropshipping, sourcing small manufacturers, and running hundreds of native-looking short-form videos a day through paid creators and repost accounts.

principles.text: Pick a product that is intrinsically viral: novelty that triggers a strong emotion drives watching and sharing.
principles.quote: making the viewer feel something and it doesn't matter what you're making them feel it just you need to make them feel like a super intense emotion

principles.text: Validate demand by spotting a product already going viral with no real brand behind it, then build the brand properly.
principles.quote: clearly they've already validated that it can go viral

principles.text: Make UGC look native to the platform and trends, not like an ad, or viewers skip it.
principles.quote: I try to make them seem as native as possible consumers are smart if they think it's an app they're not going to watch it

principles.text: Scale content volume: many creators and a web of reposter accounts posting daily, then put paid spend behind proven winners.
principles.quote: I take my most model creatives and play these meme pages that have tens of millions of followers to post my content

principles.text: Build a brand, not a dropshipping shop: community and identity create repeat customers and exit equity.
principles.quote: the people that make money I'm talking real money they don't make it off the cash flow they don't make it off the yearly sales they're making it off the exit

principles.text: Find small manufacturers by brute-force outreach: search deep, log them in a spreadsheet, and call and email everyone.
principles.quote: I literally typed in on Google chocolate contract manufacturer I went through all the pages on Google like the first 20 or 25 pages I made a spreadsheet

sources.title: Oliver Brocato's no-ad-spend organic playbook: TikTok creator studios, meme pages, micro-influencers
sources.originalTitle: The Marketing Strategy That Made Me $10 MILLION (no ad spend)
sources.summary: Oliver Brocato explains the three organic pillars (content creators, meme pages, influencers) behind his $10M revenue with zero paid ads. The core engine is a high-volume TikTok content studio of many creators on rev-share, using a controversy post plus reply-to-comment sales videos, then repurposing via affiliates.

principles.text: Organic growth rests on three pillars: content creators, meme pages, and micro-influencers.
principles.quote: there are three pillars first is content creators second are memes and third are influencers

principles.text: Success on TikTok is quantity times quality; don't judge organic before making hundreds of videos.
principles.quote: quantity times quality equals success a lot of people focus on the quality part and they ignore the quantity part if you've made less than 500 videos quit the crying

principles.text: Hire many creators to run brand accounts instead of making content yourself or micromanaging scripts; cut low performers, double down on winners.
principles.quote: higher quality Talent cut the low performers and double down on the people that are pushing views

principles.text: Align creators with a small base retainer plus a big affiliate share (about 20%) so their pay tracks performance.
principles.quote: a super small base retainer ultimately I offer them a huge affiliate percentage twenty percent of all sales that they generate by doing so it aligns our interests

principles.text: Use a one-two punch: a controversial top-of-funnel video for eyeballs, then reply-to-comment videos where you sell hard on features and objections.
principles.quote: punch number two is Boom the hook that comes from the right side that right there are the replying to combat videos you make videos responding to comments on the original viral video

principles.text: Rent meme-page distribution for 24-hour link-in-bio posts at $100-$500 instead of paying for ads; and use micro-influencers at scale without scripting.
principles.quote: you're able to pay the owners a hundred bucks 300 bucks 500 bucks for 20 four hour post

sources.title: How I built a $10M-run-rate Shopify chocolate brand: viral demand, creator retainers, and surviving setbacks
sources.originalTitle: How I Built A $10,000,000 Shopify Chocolate Business
sources.summary: Oliver Brocato recounts taking a single-product chocolate brand from zero to $3M in year one, then through a stockout, bans and a co-founder exit. Key lessons: pick products by marketability, replace one-off influencers with retained creators on dedicated accounts, and invest in packaging and team.

principles.text: Choose a product for its potential to be marketed, not for the product itself.
principles.quote: it really wasn't too much about the product but more so the potential to Market it

principles.text: Reframe a taboo category into a luxury experience through branding and packaging, which drives acquisition.
principles.quote: The Branding and packaging is what helps us acquire the customers at the end of the day

principles.text: Product quality drives retention: if the experience is bad, customers never return.
principles.quote: if the chocolate isn't good and they don't have a good experience they're never going to come back

principles.text: One-off influencer deals spike sales then fall to zero, and cold outreach converts poorly, so they can't build stability.
principles.quote: I would post and sales would go up and they would spike and then they would fall back down close to zero

principles.text: Pay creators a flat retainer to post daily on dedicated brand-run accounts instead of renting influencer audiences.
principles.quote: I hired a key on a retainer basis I paid him a flat fee to make one Tick Tock a day for 30 days

principles.text: Scale by giving each creator their own independent account, since TikTok rewards good content rather than follower count.
principles.quote: it wasn't about how many followers you had but rather could you make good content hit the for you pitch

sources.title: How Oliver Brocato went from fidget spinners to a $5M brand by 21: his story, year by year
sources.originalTitle: 0 to $5 million at 21 years old. My Story.
sources.summary: Oliver walks through his path from age 14 to 21: fidget spinners, a social media agency, failed dropshipping and Etsy chargebacks, consulting for a Blazer brand, TikTok influencer growth, and a viral leggings brand. Each stage built a skill (distribution, attribution, paid ads, influencer buying) that set up his chocolate brand.

principles.text: When a local market saturates, expand to a bigger channel (he moved from in-person fidget spinner sales to eBay).
principles.quote: I inevitably saturated the in-person market and so I kind of had this realization like the only way to really grow this and expand this and so the obvious path was listed on eBay

principles.text: Learn measurable paid ads: attribution lets you prove real revenue impact, which makes you hard to replace.
principles.quote: if I could go to a store owner or a brand owner and drive real impact and drive real Revenue I knew that I would be Untouchable

principles.text: Weak online presence means big easy wins; basic optimizations alone can multiply sales.
principles.quote: first month we went from 400 a day in sales to like three thousand dollars a day and while I'd love to take credit for that I will say a lot of these things were like super basic optimizations

principles.text: Being early on a new platform is an edge: creators hadn't monetized yet, so brand deals were cheap.
principles.quote: influencers had never monetized on Tick Tock before which meant that you were able to get brand deals for pennies on the dollar

principles.text: Buy distribution, not brand name: mid-size influencers deliver reach at a fraction of the price.
principles.quote: you're not paying for their brand name but rather you're paying for the distribution

principles.text: To deliver a great service, build a team of specialists rather than doing everything yourself.
principles.quote: I needed to build the tea I need to build infrastructure and bring in killers in their respective fields in order to provide an amazing service

sources.title: How Tabs Chocolates hit $9M with no paid ads: viral product plus a high-volume creator flywheel
sources.originalTitle: From $0 to $10M in 12 Month NO Ad Spend | Oliver Brocato | Tabs Chocolates
sources.summary: Oliver Brocato explains how Tabs did about $9M at a 40% net margin using only organic short-form video. He covers building a product primed for virality, running hundreds of creator-owned TikTok accounts on a hybrid retainer plus revenue-share deal, and recycling winners through meme pages and a Discord of reposters.

principles.text: Organic scale only works if the product itself is built for virality; distribution tactics can't fix a commodity.
principles.quote: the key takeaway here is that nothing else works all the strategies that I'm going to tell you about today they will not work unless you have some sort of features in your product or a product that is built and Prime for virality

principles.text: Win on volume: put out enough short-form content and systemize it so output runs passively.
principles.quote: if we put out enough short form we will inevitably win it's just a matter of systemizing it

principles.text: Give each creator their own account so you can read analytics per creator and reach distinct audiences.
principles.quote: I wanted to basically segment out the creators onto different pages so I'd be able to understand what the analytics looked like

principles.text: Pay creators a small retainer plus revenue share, keeping upfront cash low.
principles.quote: that ends up coming out to about $500 to $1,000 a month in cash and then I give them 20% of all revenue that they

principles.text: Hand creators past winning concepts and creative freedom instead of scripts; proven virality repeats.
principles.quote: give them the winning Concepts because what goes viral once will go viral again

principles.text: Use two hooks: aim every video at virality first, then convert the attention with comment-reply videos that push the product.
principles.quote: once again the goal is to get a viral video and then it's to capitalize on the viral video with responding to comment videos

sources.title: Oliver Brocato on reps, personal brand and compounding experience after building a sex chocolate brand
sources.originalTitle: How I ACTUALLY built a $10,000,000 Chocolate Empire
sources.summary: Oliver tells his story from fidget spinners to a multi-million chocolate brand, a near-collapse in July 2022, and what he learned. Core lessons: define goals, stack reps, build a personal brand on Twitter for team and network, and share unfiltered stories. Light on tactics, strong on mindset.

principles.text: Define your goal and obsess over it; then execute, because clarity precedes action.
principles.quote: if you define your goal and you embody your goal and you think about your goal and you obsess over your goal that over time you're going to reach a goal

principles.text: Success comes from experience and intuition built through many failed reps, not IQ.
principles.quote: what leads to success is not like IQ or intelligence it's experience and intuition experience is seeing all the different situations and seeing how things play out and falling into every single Pitfall and failing

principles.text: The game gets easier as you advance: network access shares insider info early.
principles.quote: dude there's so much Alpha and sauce that gets shared like once you reach a certain point

principles.text: A small, high-quality Twitter following beats a big generic one; it sources team and relationships.
principles.quote: my 21 000 followers is more powerful than most Instagram thoughts have with three million I'm not kidding because the quality of followers that I have are unbelievable

principles.text: Build in public with the good and the bad; transparency creates connection.
principles.quote: everybody talks about the wins the dubs like you know making abs like the vacations the girls the bottles and this the that right like that's cool but I think that like what really kind of creates that connection um is when you go a level deeper

principles.text: Ride trends early and optimize marketplace listings with competitor keywords and review prompts.
principles.quote: since I was so early on in the trend and I was like smart enough you know like I would you know I was I was optimizing my listing I was looking at competitors and the keywords that they were using I would use similar keywords

sources.title: How Tabs Chocolate went from banned on every ad platform to $5M with TikTok organic and affiliate armies
sources.originalTitle: Oliver Brocato: Tabs Chocolate, $5 Million Shopify Journey, And More | Arie Scherson Podcast #23
sources.summary: Oliver Brocato explains how Tabs Chocolate grew with no paid ads. He moved from one-off influencers to one-creator-per-account TikTok pages, then added a 2,000-person affiliate Discord. He also covers why experience compounds into intuition, why focus beats jumping between projects, and how a public build-in-public Twitter journey brings in inbound deals.

principles.text: Don't stack creators on one TikTok account; scale horizontally with one creator per brand account.
principles.quote: scale horizontally across multiple accounts bringing on multiple independent creators matching it one Creator per one account

principles.text: One-off influencer posts give spikes then zero. Build a repeatable system for a baseline instead.
principles.quote: we would see the post would go up Revenue would spike and then as soon as like you know things start to chill off Revenue would be back at zero

principles.text: Gamify an affiliate Discord with commissions, base pay and raffles to multiply content distribution.
principles.quote: they get a 20 Commission on any sell that they make

principles.text: Beginners should learn TikTok organic: it takes almost no money to go from zero to six or seven figures.
principles.quote: familiarize yourself with Tick Tock organic um like learn learn that skill

principles.text: Document your journey publicly and the best clients come inbound; do exceptional work and partners line up.
principles.quote: all of our clients have been inbound man um you know since since I started tabs um about like two years ago um I've been like documenting my whole entire Journey on Twitter

principles.text: Eight-figure operators aren't smarter; their repeated reps build intuition. Stay on one thing long enough to compound.
principles.quote: it boils down to to your experience which leads to intuition which leads to success

sources.title: How Oliver Brocato growth-hacks a B2B SaaS (Bustem) off a Twitter following and ROI-framed pricing
sources.originalTitle: E29: Growth Hacking Your First SAAS with Oliver Brocato
sources.summary: Oliver Brocato, who exited Tabs Chocolate and now runs Bustem (anti-counterfeit takedowns for ecom brands), explains how he reuses a 50k-person audience as distribution, frames every message in dollars recovered, and prices with a performance model that upsells into an unlimited retainer. He also contrasts consumer and B2B growth.

principles.text: Point an existing audience at your own offer instead of promoting other people's products as an affiliate.
principles.quote: might as well like have my own sort of offer and build my own business off the back of my distribution.

principles.text: A personal brand built in public is a launch weapon: it delivered signups and booked calls on day one and every day after.
principles.quote: I put out a tweet that, you know, got over 250,000 impressions and like over 400 signups like in our first day

principles.text: Tie every message and product surface to dollars lost and recovered so the buyer sees it as P&L, not a nice-to-have.
principles.quote: everything that we do we try to connect it back to like here's how much revenue you're losing

principles.text: An ROI claim only works if it is transparent and verifiable; a bare multiple isn't believable.
principles.quote: just slapping a 10x ROI isn't good enough. Like you got to you got to go a step further.

principles.text: Price with a low-commitment performance tier that customers outgrow into an unlimited retainer on their own.
principles.quote: the all you can eat sort of unlimited retainer becomes an ascension that people opt into voluntarily

principles.text: Make outbound specific and curiosity-driven by leading with the concrete problem you found about the prospect.
principles.quote: hey like we found over 200 copycats counterfeits that are like ripping you off. Do you want to see the list?

sources.title: Why Oliver builds in public and his 2024 plan: scale a personal brand and an AI study tool through a growth plateau
sources.originalTitle: How I'm Gonna Make 1 Million Dollars In 2024
sources.summary: Oliver explains why building in public increases "surface area for luck," then lays out his 2024 plan: scale his personal brand (over $40k/month) into a media company and push his AI study tool from about $25k to $250k MRR. He is candid about being stuck on paid acquisition and the persistence mindset he's using to push through the plateau.

principles.text: A personal brand multiplies your surface area for luck and opportunity; building in public opens doors to advisers, investors, and talent.
principles.quote: by establishing a personal brand you increase your surface area for luck and opportunity like nothing else

principles.text: A public audience is a fast talent and help network: one post can surface designers, ad experts, or fixes within seconds.
principles.quote: I can tweet anything absolutely anything like you know I need a Google ads guy or my Facebook ad account got banned or if if anybody knows a good designer hit me up and in a matter of seconds I have scores of messages

principles.text: Turn a personal brand into a real business by expanding to new platforms and formats: YouTube, short form, newsletter, in-person events.
principles.quote: I want to expand into new avenues and platforms and start building audiences out on new channels

principles.text: If organic growth continues despite churn and no ad spend, you have product-market signal; the remaining problem is finding acquisition channels.
principles.quote: we've been growing month over month organically from anywhere between 3 to 7% so we know that this you know product [ __ ] works

principles.text: When ad accounts get banned, test many channels in parallel: meme pages, micro and macro influencers, and different paid platforms.
principles.quote: testing out me Pages testing out influencers micro influencers macro influencers people with millions of followers Tik tokers instagrammers YouTubers testing out different paid ads platforms

principles.text: Treat plateaus like a woodpecker on a tree: keep hitting consistently, because the breakthrough comes on one more hit.
principles.quote: we're that woodpecker right that's like hitting the [ __ ] tree hitting the tree hitting the tree and we've hit the tree like a hundred times and all it's going to take is like 101 or 102 or 103

sources.title: How Tabs Chocolate engineered virality: volume posting, creator "franchises", and a product built to go viral
sources.originalTitle: Ep 218: Tabs Sex Chocolate: Engineering Virality from Day One
sources.summary: Oliver Brocato explains how Tabs reached seven figures in year one with no paid ads. They designed a product that explains itself on camera, obsessed over launch details, then flooded TikTok, Reels and Shorts with content through creators on retainer running branded sub-accounts.

principles.text: Pick products that can go viral and sell themselves, with real barriers to entry, before spending on growth.
principles.quote: we had two pieces of criteria that we really wanted to kind of meet one being a product that can go viral and sell itself and two a product that has high barriers to entry and a level of proprietary nature around it

principles.text: Perfect the brand, design, unboxing and site before launch; agonize over every micro detail.
principles.quote: we wanted to ensure that before we launched we had everything perfect from the branding the design the unboxing experience the website we agonized over every single micro detail

principles.text: You can't predict which video goes viral, so win on volume at a quality baseline: buy the whole haystack.
principles.quote: it's not about picking the needle in the haystack it's about you know buying the whole haystack

principles.text: Put good creators on retainer and have them run branded sub-accounts, turning them into franchisees and locking in distribution.
principles.quote: we started to put good creators and influencers on retainer and we would have them post for us on a recurring basis they would post on their own page and then we would run subsidiary and secondary pages on tick tock

principles.text: When a video pops, double down fast; a follow-up reply to a comment with a call to action can outperform the original.
principles.quote: the secondary post responding to a comment on the original viral video will actually do better than the viral video itself despite getting like 1 10th 1 20th of the number of views

principles.text: Design the product so its concept is understood in seconds on camera; the clean-break chocolate square does this.
principles.quote: it explains the concept of what it is in a three second you know uh visual way without having to provide you know like paragraphs and essays of context

sources.title: How Tabs Chocolate hit $2.5M in year one with a TikTok-first product and multi-account creator system
sources.originalTitle: Selling Sex Chocolate On Tiktok | Tabs Chocolate Founder Oliver Brocato | NMT EP14
sources.summary: Oliver Brocato explains how he built a viral-by-design product, then scaled organic TikTok with creators on retainer, one per account, plus a Discord affiliate army. He also covers the dropshipping-to-brand ladder, hiring lessons, and where organic stops working.

principles.text: Engineer the product to be viral on the target platform; repackage proven ingredients in a new, visual format rather than inventing something new.
principles.quote: we took the most popular and effective of natural supplements and just put it in a new form right so it's not like we came up like with this crazy recipe or concoction

principles.text: Break-in-half packaging makes the product explain itself on camera, which makes content easier to make and share.
principles.quote: that also plays extremely well on camera it's like visually explains the prodct

principles.text: Organic TikTok is a volume game: you can't predict the winner, so publish enough that one hits.
principles.quote: if we put up 50 videos in a day one will hit

principles.text: Put one creator on one brand account and scale horizontally; stacking creators on a page confuses the algorithm.
principles.quote: I isolated one Creator per one account and like scale horizontally across what I like to call like subsidiary accounts

principles.text: Influencer outreach is mostly ghosting and high rates; hiring creators on retainer to run brand pages scales better.
principles.quote: businesses hire a Creator to run a brand page so I'm going to do that and then I'm going to keep scaling that across more brand pages with more creatives

principles.text: Treat entrepreneurship as a ladder: dropshipping, then private label, then a proprietary product with barriers and a moat.
principles.quote: it's a ladder you know it's like you know you start off with Drop Shipping You Learn you learn skills

sources.title: Oliver Brocato: from fidget spinners to an $11M TikTok chocolate brand, and why to pick one business and stick to it
sources.originalTitle: Waking up at 5 AM and taking cold showers isn't the only way to succeed
sources.summary: Oliver Brocato, a 21-year-old e-commerce founder, explains how years of small ventures led to TABS, a sexually enhancing chocolate built for TikTok that he scaled to about $11M a year. He covers sticking with one business through the early slump, focusing on the first customers, picking the right vehicle, and building a personal brand.

principles.text: Beat shiny object syndrome: pick one business and see it through, because breakthroughs take years and most people quit at the first slump.
principles.quote: the important thing is that you pick one and you stick to it and you see it through because like that is the only way you're going to see the light at the end of the tunnel

principles.text: Early on, ignore the big dream and obsess over the next handful of customers; confidence and momentum follow from each small win.
principles.quote: how do I get my first five customers you got that boom now I'm more confident how do I get my first 50. how do I get my first 500 and then again you let momentum like do the work for you

principles.text: The business you choose matters more than your skill: a great operator can't take a weak product far, while an average one with the right opportunity can rocket.
principles.quote: the vehicle or the business that you choose is actually more important than your ability as an entrepreneur

principles.text: Start from something already viral and build the business around it, designing the product for the channel (TikTok) rather than finding a channel for a product.
principles.quote: I decided to take something that was already viral

principles.text: Early-stage platforms are a distribution arbitrage: creators who haven't monetized yet take deals for almost nothing and audiences aren't saturated with ads.
principles.quote: influencers had never monetized on the platform which meant that you can basically secure deals like for pennies on the dollar

principles.text: Build a personal brand for leverage and access, but stay a business operator first so the content is a byproduct of real work.
principles.quote: as soon as you're on people's Radars like your luck just increases a hundred fold

sources.title: How Oliver Brocato built TABS Chocolate for virality: creator networks, hybrid pay, diversified channels
sources.originalTitle: Viral Marketing with Oliver Brocato (creator of TABS Chocolate)
sources.summary: Oliver Brocato explains why he designed TABS around short-form virality instead of marketing an existing product. He covers scaling with many creator-run pages, moving to hybrid retainer plus revenue share, diversifying channels, using packaging for first purchase, and using a personal brand for hiring and networking.

principles.text: Design the product to go viral itself instead of trying to market an existing product.
principles.quote: I want to build a product that can go viral by itself and so you know that's what tabs is

principles.text: Make the product instantly understandable in a few seconds so short-form creators can demo it easily.
principles.quote: you're able to kind of understand how it works in like a 3 second like snippet or sound bite

principles.text: Scale creator content horizontally: many creators, each running their own independent brand page, rather than stacking creators on one page.
principles.quote: instead of bringing on more content creators adding them to the page I expanded horizontally bringing on as many creators as I possibly could and setting them up with their own independent page

principles.text: Pay creators a small retainer plus a percentage of upside, since pure affiliate is hard to recruit for.
principles.quote: a hybrid of like super small retainer enough where like they're happy if nothing happens yeah um but you know not a crazy amount of money and then giving them a percentage of all the upside

principles.text: Avoid reliance on one channel; build many channels so small incremental lifts compound.
principles.quote: instead of being over reliant on one channel when you're like an octopus and you have your tentacles on 12 different channels

principles.text: Packaging wins the first purchase, but product quality drives repeat orders and word of mouth.
principles.quote: the packaging is what gets us to acquire the first customer now if the product isn't good the customer is not coming back

sources.title: The AI SaaS Ads Playbook: Oliver Brocato on paid ads, testing, LTV and distribution for SaaS
sources.originalTitle: The AI SaaS Ads Playbook | Oliver Brocato | SaaS Sauce Ep. 2
sources.summary: Oliver Brocato explains how he picks products and channels that fit his edge, borrows proven ideas, and wins paid ads through a strong back-end (LTV, pricing, upsells) and heavy creative testing. He also covers channel-product fit, in-person distribution and super affiliates for his e-commerce brand-protection SaaS.

principles.text: Build in spaces where you hold a distribution edge, and pick products that suit your core skill.
principles.quote: I like to play I like to play in spaces that I have an edge in.

principles.text: Let others validate the market, then improve one thing; existing competitors are signal, not a stop sign.
principles.quote: I think it's important to let other people do the groundwork and the heavy lifting and the validating for you.

principles.text: Ads win on the back-end machine (pricing tests, flows, upsells), not on a copied creative. Higher LTV lets you afford higher CAC.
principles.quote: if I don't have like the machine that you've spent you know years building out. I could run the same ad as you.

principles.text: Scaling ads from six to seven figures comes down to creative and volume testing, then remaking winning angles with many creators and hooks.
principles.quote: in order to scale from like six figures a month to seven figures a month and like really do big boy numbers is it all comes down to like creative testing like and volume testing

principles.text: Test many channels fast, fail quickly, and go all in when one shows a sliver of traction; the product shapes which channel works.
principles.quote: the biggest principles is test test test try try see something that works 100x double down on it and and go all in on it.

principles.text: Recruit a few well-networked super affiliates (agency or software owners); one rolodex can beat ads or cold email.
principles.quote: One guy like that with that kind of a rolodex and book of business is worth like, you know, a lot like way more than like Facebook ads or cold email.

sources.title: How Oliver Brocato went from Tabs to Bustm: B2B pricing, personal brand growth and zero churn
sources.originalTitle: How Oliver Brocato Saves E-commerce Brands MILLIONS (EASY)
sources.summary: Oliver Brocato explains moving from a viral consumer brand (Tabs) to B2B software (Bustm), including how he fixed pricing by switching to a performance model with a monitoring fee. He covers founder-led growth through his Twitter, word of mouth, and why a good product beats marketing machines in B2B.

principles.text: In B2B, a genuinely good product is the biggest growth hack because customers talk and refer each other.
principles.quote: in the B2B space like having a good product is like the biggest growth hack, right?

principles.text: Founder personal brand and content can be the main acquisition channel; Oliver is hiring a full-time shadow writer to scale it.
principles.quote: I am my marketing. Like, dude, it's me like talking about it and tweeting it and talking about my journey and talking about case studies and success stories

principles.text: Build a business that grows on word of mouth instead of one that needs constant ad spend to buy revenue.
principles.quote: a business that can survive off of like word of mouth and grow off of word of mouth is a way more value business than like one where you need to like dump a dollar in to get like a $120 out

principles.text: High retainers make clients hypersensitive to results; a performance-based downsell converted far better and cut resentment.
principles.quote: when you charge people a lot of money like they're very sensitive to you like are you getting results you're not getting results

principles.quote: If you're willing to pay something then you'll be willing to take stuff down and got rid of the time wasters

principles.text: Zoom out on setbacks; short-term swings feel catastrophic but the long-run trend is what matters, so keep marching forward.
principles.quote: when you fixate on like a particular hour or moment or day sometimes it feels like it's like the end of the world.

principles.text: Learn to get attention and distribution; it matters more than the business model you pick.
principles.quote: if you want to like make a lot of money online, like you need to master and understand like how to get impressions and views and drive clicks through, you know, social media.

principles.text: In ecom, ad creative is the biggest lever; in B2B software, the founder's personal brand is the cheat code.
principles.quote: the biggest cheat code of B2B software is a founder personal brand

principles.text: Don't invent something novel. Start from a validated idea, then tweak, iterate and improve it.
principles.quote: you need to like do something that has some sort of like validation behind it and then you know tweak it, iterate on it, improve it.

principles.text: Prospects already using a competitor are better leads: they have a problem and a budget.
principles.quote: if they're working with our competitor it means they have a problem. It means that they have a budget for the problem.

principles.text: Don't give the product away free. Paying customers have skin in the game and give real feedback.
principles.quote: you want people that are bought in and have skin in the game.

principles.text: Build around one micro-niche pain point, solved extremely well, rather than an everything app.
principles.quote: you want to find like one problem and then solve for that one problem, right?

sources.title: How Oliver Brocato built Bustem, a brand-protection service, after copycats nearly bankrupted his chocolate brand
sources.originalTitle: Meet The 21 y/o Genius That Changed Ecom Forever | Oliver Brocato (Bustem) Interview
sources.summary: Oliver Brocato explains how counterfeits and copycats nearly bankrupted his chocolate brand, then how he built Bustem to fight them. Bustem is a hybrid of AI automation and human analysts sold as a roughly $3k/month retainer. He covers productizing a services business, free audits as the sales motion, and who should and shouldn't buy.

principles.text: Build the product for the pain you lived through as an operator, especially when you see no existing solutions.
principles.quote: Copycats, counterfeits, and unauthorized resellers was a massive pain point uh that we dealt with that almost bankrupted the company multiple times.

principles.text: Combine human experts with automation to deliver a service-grade outcome at an affordable flat retainer.
principles.quote: we've done a really interesting job of, you know, building a solution that combines real human labor and and people and experts with automation and technology to tackle this problem for a very affordable couple thousand a month retainer.

principles.text: Customers often don't want software to operate; they want the outcome handled, so deliver white-glove service on a productized backend.
principles.quote: What we found is that clients don't want to even log into the platform or be bogged down inside of a software. They just want this handled all for them.

principles.text: Lead sales with free value: run the audit before the call and give it away whether or not they buy.
principles.quote: we will compile all the threats that we found and we'll walk you through what we find on the call. We'll show you that. We'll give it to you whether you work with us or not.

principles.text: Qualify ruthlessly: tell small brands to go scale first, and sell to businesses where the problem is already material.
principles.quote: you have to be a brand that's doing more than $100,000 a month. If you're doing less than that like I always tell founders like you got bigger problems to worry about

principles.text: Attack the weak points of the supporting infrastructure, not the bad actor, because the intermediaries respond to liability.
principles.quote: we basically attack the infrastructure that supports a bad guy. So, we go after the domain, the registar, the hosting provider, the payment processor in order to effectively get the bad guy removed and taken down.

sources.title: Copycat brands: how to spot them and five ways to stop them
sources.originalTitle: Copycat brands: how to spot and stop them
sources.summary: An essay by Bustem's founder on how to tell original brands from copycats and what to do when you're copied: audit your IP, register trademarks, differentiate on customer focus, confront professionally, and out-innovate imitators. Argues copycats compete on features while authentic brands build on emotional connection, loyalty and speed.

principles.text: Being copied signals your product is worth copying; reframe the anger, then run a systematic IP audit before calling lawyers.
principles.quote: your business model, branding, or products are successful enough to warrant copying. As the saying goes, imitation is the sincerest form of flattery.

principles.text: Defend your brand before it's attacked: register trademarks and copyrights early and keep dated records of every asset, launch and market entry.
principles.quote: The brands that successfully fend off copycats aren't those that react to infringement—they're the ones that anticipated it and built comprehensive protection systems before problems emerged.

principles.text: Pick your enforcement battles: fight when revenue, confusion or your registered marks are hit; just monitor when similarity is superficial or enforcement costs more than the harm.
principles.quote: Not every instance of copying warrants aggressive legal action. Experienced brand owners develop judgment about which battles matter

principles.text: Stay obsessed with the customer, not the imitator; time spent on copycats is time your advantage erodes, and copycats can't copy relationships, culture or story.
principles.quote: The moment you spend more time obsessing over imitators than serving your customers is the moment your competitive advantage begins eroding.

principles.text: Feature-led positioning is a short-term model because competitors catch up; build the message on the customer's emotional state before and after purchase.
principles.quote: Even though it is smart to focus on features the marketplace needs to include, it is a short-term business model, as others will want to catch up.

principles.text: Keep innovating faster than copycats can replicate; a rapid release cycle makes copying economically unattractive and widens the gap over time.
principles.quote: by the time they've successfully replicated your current offering, you've already moved on to the next generation.

sources.title: Brand protection: how to defend against counterfeits and copycats
sources.originalTitle: How to protect your brand from counterfeits
sources.summary: Bustem founder Oliver Brocato explains how e-commerce brands can defend against counterfeits. Register your IP first, enforce takedowns on platforms rather than litigate, monitor at scale because infringers keep reappearing, tighten the supply chain, and educate customers.

principles.text: Register your IP first. It lets you prove ownership when you find fakes.
principles.quote: Registering your intellectual property is the most elementary step in protecting your brand from counterfeits.

principles.text: Detect infringement early. Speed protects profits, goodwill and market position.
principles.quote: The sooner you detect and stop the violation, the better chance you will have to protect your profits, business or product’s goodwill, and overall market position.

principles.text: Prefer platform takedowns over lawsuits when the goal is fast removal. Litigation is slow, costly and uncertain.
principles.quote: Going through litigation is time-consuming and expensive, and there is no guarantee of success.

principles.text: One takedown doesn't end it. Counterfeiters relist across marketplaces and countries, so enforce at scale with technology.
principles.quote: Online brands often play whack-a-mole with counterfeiters because infringers place fake listings on multiple marketplaces across many countries.

principles.text: Close supply chain gaps with strong supplier contracts and traceability so counterfeiters can't exploit them.
principles.quote: Ensure strong supplier contracts and maintain traceability in your supply chain to prevent any form of weakness that counterfeiters could exploit.

principles.text: Educate customers on legitimate channels and how to spot and report fakes to rebuild trust.
principles.quote: Take another step forward at countering counterfeit products by educating your customers on the benefits of opting for legitimate products and the channels where they can find these.

sources.title: Brand protection strategies: 13 tactics for defending against copycats and counterfeits
sources.originalTitle: Brand protection strategies
sources.summary: A founder-written checklist for protecting a brand from counterfeits and copycats: register IP and domains, monitor continuously, enforce fast, use AI detection, and revisit the plan regularly. It is partly a content piece for Bustem, so the value is in the practical sequence of protect, monitor, enforce and iterate.

principles.text: Brand protection never ends once trademarks and domains are registered; ongoing monitoring catches infringement before it hurts.
principles.quote: Brand protection doesn’t stop once you've registered trademarks or domain names. Continuous ongoing monitoring is essential to detect potential infringements early on before they harm your brand.

principles.text: Build protection into the brand from day one, since strong recognition and consistent branding deter copycats as you grow.
principles.quote: Consider brand protection as you build the brand itself, and make sure your brand management team is on the same page as you.

principles.text: When infringement happens, act quickly and escalate in steps: cease and desist, platform enforcement, then legal action.
principles.quote: Despite your best efforts, it’s still likely that infringement could occur. When it does, it’s essential to act quickly and decisively.

principles.text: Automate detection with AI tools so your time goes to legal action and strategy, not manual searching.
principles.quote: You can also do it manually, but why waste time when you have tools to do it for you, while you focus on legal actions and strategy development?

principles.text: DIY enforcement leaks; specialist agencies provide constant monitoring and platform relationships that let fewer infringements slip through.
principles.quote: It requires constant checking, and letting some infringement slip through the cracks when you go the DIY route is easy.

principles.text: Treat the strategy as a living plan: track incidents, response times and resolutions, and refine as new threats emerge.
principles.quote: You can’t just set your brand protection strategy and forget about it.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Oliver Brocato explains how he built Tabs, a sex-chocolate brand, by designing the product to go viral on TikTok. He covers running hundreds of independent creator accounts, the one-two punch of viral video plus comment-reply retargeting, funnel upsells that double AOV, and price testing.

chunks.heading: Oliver's product thesis: build something intrinsically viral, then reverse-engineer the brand
chunks.text:
- Oliver argues dropshipping is "a bit of a scam" as a beginner entry point. It is arguably harder than building a real brand, because you are always chasing the next fad and the next buck.
- Dropshipping gives a poor customer experience, so there is no LTV. You must be profitable on the first sale, with no room to play with acquisition cost.
- A real brand expects a customer to return 10 to 20 times over 5 to 10 years, which gives margin to spend on acquisition up front.
- He says "the real wealth comes from the exit, not from the cash flow." Every dollar of brand profit is worth 3 to 5x at exit, which is where generational wealth is made, "not off of selling trinkets from Alibaba."
- Most founders build the product and brand first, then work out marketing. Oliver reversed it: "how do I build a product that's going to go viral?"
- Tabs (sex chocolate) genesis: he saw a similar product in a TikTok with 8M views and 2M likes. The brand behind it was not sold online, had weak packaging and no social presence. He concluded it was an intrinsically viral product that someone who knew how to execute could turn into millions.
- He says the product was chosen because he could "market the [expletive] out of this," not out of passion for the category.
- Tabs' hook is explainable in three seconds on video: the chocolate splits in half, one half per partner, so the product needs no explanation or text.
- Results he cites: over $10M revenue this year at 40 to 45% net margin, over 1B organic views, $1M+ in sales in the first six months target and about $4M in year one.

chunks.heading: Building the physical product: sourcing, moq and making complexity the moat
chunks.text:
- Oliver started with about $30,000 of savings from earlier ventures (fidget spinners, an agency, dropshipping, eBay and Etsy stores). It took 11 months from idea to first sellable product.
- Chocolate co-manufacturer search: he Googled "chocolate co-manufacturer," scraped the first 20 to 30 pages of results, and called roughly 100 companies asking about minimum order quantity (MOQ).
- Most chocolate co-manufacturers will not touch you unless you order very large runs (he cites around 2 million squares at the extreme). Fixed costs (setup, cleaning equipment) are the same for a 10,000-piece or a 10-million-piece run, so small orders are unattractive to them.
- Only one or two were viable. He picked on MOQ, pricing and samples, ordering about eight chocolates for a taste test with friends.
- His manufacturer specialized in alternative chocolates (superfood, CBD), so adding supplements was a small step. He did not invent a formula: he took the most popular natural sex supplements (usually pills or powder) and repackaged them as a luxury, destigmatized, shareable experience.
- Supply chain: about 8 manufacturers. Chocolate is made in Salt Lake City, Utah. Boxes, chrome poly mailers and custom molds come from China (boxes found on Alibaba, communication over Skype and WeChat). Boxes are labor intensive and he could not find a US maker.
- Lead times: poly mailers take about 90 days to make and ship, so he plans months ahead. If one manufacturer slips or he misorders, everything stops.
- Heat was a real problem he did not plan for: chocolate melts in summer, and customers complained when summer hit. Poly mailers that trap heat were part of the fix.
- He says the difficulty "became our moat": the barrier to entry protected him from the 300 ecom guys who copy a hot product, saturate it and rip you off.

chunks.heading: Luxury positioning, packaging and pricing
chunks.text:
- Positioning: "We're not selling chocolate, we're selling an experience, we're selling a mood." Three tiny 20-gram squares sell for $29.99 because the pitch is "the best night of your life with your loved one."
- Every decision follows one value, luxury: scarcity (only three pieces rather than 50 or 100), design and unboxing. Details include gold foil stamping, socials printed inside the lid and an emoji under each piece.
- He designed the box himself in Canva, and the manufacturer's designer cleaned it up into 3D renders. His inspiration was the Truff hot sauce box: a cheap-to-make product (truffle-infused hot sauce) sold at around $30 on branding and packaging.
- For packaging he messaged hundreds of suppliers on Alibaba and got only three or four samples.
- Pricing: launched at $19.99 with no competitor anchor, calling the number "pulled out of our ass." Pills and powders at about $10 are not comparable because Tabs sells an experience.
- When he raised the price, conversion went up, not down. He now split-tests five price points in roughly $2 steps, sending about 20% of traffic to each.
- His logic: a high price signals quality. A trainer who offers sessions for $29.99 reads as bad; one who charges a lot reads as the best. At $4.99 the chocolate would look fake.
- At scale, tiny optimizations compound. Cutting one ounce from the box drops it into a lower shipping bracket and saves over $300,000 a year at his run rate.

chunks.heading: The TikTok creator engine: retainers, many independent accounts, copying winners
chunks.text:
- Early plan was micro-influencers (50K to 200K followers, aiming for sub-$1 CPM), with free product plus small cash. It did not scale: only about 30 of every 1,000 outreach emails replied, rates were often unaffordable, creators ghosted or stole product, and sales spiked and crashed after each post.
- Breakthrough: he paid a creator named Keith, found on Twitter with zero followers, a $2,000 flat retainer for 30 TikToks a month (one a day) to run the brand account. By day five a video hit and the month produced $70K to $80K in sales. He calls this the "holy [expletive]" moment, because one creator on retainer is "set and forget" versus chasing influencers.
- To scale, he did not add creators to one account. He argues the algorithm rewards a consistent, niche style, and "too many cooks" confuse it. Instead each creator gets their own independent account.
- Creators create the accounts with their own email, password and phone number, and name them some variation of "tabs". He deliberately does not create or control the accounts, because tying many accounts to his IP risks bans. Hundreds to thousands of accounts exist.
- Casting: he hired "anybody and everybody." If they had a phone and limbs, they were in. He paid roughly $1,000 to $3,000 a month for 30 TikToks, with full creative control. The product is so viral that "even a monkey could get two million views."
- Sourcing creators: Twitter first (leveraging his personal following), then referrals (creators know other creators). Searching "UGC" on Twitter finds thousands.
- Copying: when a video goes viral he sends it to all creators to remake. "It's not about reinventing the wheel," and remakes often hit again.
- He later moved creators to commission or hybrid pay (for example 20% of tracked revenue), which limits his downside and weeds out weak ones. Tracking uses a UTM link in bio plus a discount code, run through Social Snowball.
- His mindset: "I don't want to be in charge of the TV show, I want to own the whole news channel."

chunks.heading: The one-two punch: viral video, then reply-to-comment videos that sell
chunks.text:
- Oliver says the viral video is not what drives most sales. The follow-up videos do.
- Step one: optimize for eyeballs and top-of-funnel awareness. TikTok has the cheapest CPMs.
- Step two: respond to comments on the viral video with new TikToks. From the same account, this retargets the original viewers for free. In those videos you sell hard: address pain points and objections, say where to shop, and push urgency.
- Example: a video with over 30M views produced about $40K in sales that day, and the reply videos produced $130K the next day. A week of reply videos took that month to close to seven figures.
- He stumbled on it when a creator tried reply videos and he saw his live dashboard spike by about 800.
- He says this is specific to TikTok and he has not seen it work like that on Instagram.

chunks.heading: Repurposing and paid distribution: Discord affiliate army and meme pages
chunks.text:
- Winning TikToks are archived without the watermark (using a downloader) and given a second life on Instagram Reels, YouTube Shorts, Facebook Reels and Pinterest idea pins.
- A VA with 15 accounts per platform worked at first (a Facebook Reel reached 8M views and about $30K in sales in a day, at zero ad spend), but the platforms noticed one IP and banned the accounts.
- Fix: a "make money online" Discord that started at 5 members and now has over 2,500. Members each set up their own accounts, get the profile picture, bio instructions and the library of viral videos, and post daily. They earn 20% of sales, tracked through Social Snowball.
- He gamified it: a gym-selfie channel, daily reactions fed into a wheel that pays three random members, and invite tournaments paying $100, $50 and $25 to the top three inviters. Some creators now promote the Discord rather than the product, plus shout-out swaps with other Discords.
- He says it has generated millions in revenue. A 14-year-old posting the same videos as everyone else drove about $50K in revenue, and Oliver says the algorithm is a black box: "nobody [expletive] knows," so scale wins.
- Paid distribution, not traditional ads: he pays meme pages with millions of followers to post already-viral content for 24 hours (about $100 to $2,000 per post depending on US engagement). He spends six figures a month on this and says it is profitable.
- On Twitter, a paid native viral tweet is followed a few hours later by a reply tweet like "I just found their website." He keeps it native because "if it feels like an ad it's not going to work."

chunks.heading: Maximizing AOV and LTV: funnel steps, melting insurance, SMS and tech stack
chunks.text:
- Without the funnel, average order value would be about $25. Each step adds 5% to 20% and together roughly doubles it. His logic: two stores with the same 100 visitors can make $50 versus $500, so the winner is whoever extracts the most while keeping the experience good.
- Sequence:
  - Product page: one-time purchase only, with 1, 2 or 3 box options (2 boxes: free shipping and a discount; 3 boxes: bigger discount). He found that putting subscriptions here made buyers pick one box plus subscribe instead of 2 or 3 boxes.
  - Cart: "melting insurance" at $4.99, framed as a no-brainer (replacement, money-back guarantee, skip the queue, faster shipping). The take rate is over 80%, and the cost is near zero because he replaced melted chocolate for free anyway.
  - Checkout (Shopify Plus): upgrade to subscription for 20% off.
  - Post-purchase: one-click upsell for another box at 50% off via a Shopify app (OCU), then another upsell on the thank-you page, then emails nudging non-subscribers to subscribe.
- Stack: Klaviyo for email; OneText for SMS; Shopify Plus (about $2,000/month, saving on transaction fees); One Click Upsells; Social Snowball; Trello; Slack for the whole business; Shopify analytics and Google Analytics (no Triple Whale since he runs no ads).
- OneText: Oliver says it lets customers buy inside a text and stores the card. Because abandoned-cart texts are treated as part of the same transaction, he says he can text every abandoner rather than only the roughly 20% who opted into marketing, which he says "5x'd" that reach.
- Creator tracking started as a VA-maintained spreadsheet he reviewed monthly before paying, and later moved to a software tool for views and followers. His philosophy: more creators, more affiliates, more scale.
- Next moves he lists: open to international orders (over 40% of traffic is international), diversify from 99% Shopify D2C to Amazon, Etsy and Walmart, then wholesale and retail (gas stations, smoke shops, sex shops, hotels), and new flavors, moods and lines (shroom, delta-9 CBD, functional foods).

chunks.heading: Mindset, team and personal brand
chunks.text:
- Do not put successful people on pedestals. He says the gap is experience, not intelligence: "it's about experience, it's about at-bats." He had about 20 failed ventures first and says "you can't cheat that, there is no shortcut."
- He is skeptical of college: he took a gap year, calls the business classes a joke and says he can return to school. He says many young people are being eaten by the system and that four years spent building a business beats a degree.
- His low point: in July sales fell as accounts were banned, his co-founder stepped back to school, and he moved back home to Tampa, isolated and depressed. It forced him to build a team and systems, and revenue went from about $60K a month in July to over $1M a month. Travel in Europe helped him recover. His takeaway: you cannot run a brand if you are not excited about life.
- Team: 8 to 12 core people, all contractors or agencies, mostly found via Twitter. He prefers few people and notes talent is attracted by a personal brand, and says "your business's value is the sum total of the average IQ of your business."
- Personal brand: only about 20,000 Twitter followers, yet it brought investor DMs, talent offering to work free, events and access. He is investing in YouTube and says it is not monetized but worth it for relationships and information.
- He charges $300 for 30 minutes of consulting to filter serious (seven- and eight-figure) operators, and says paying more is also a luxury-brand effect for courses.
- He warns against course gurus with rented Lamborghinis and small real profits, but says legit courses and masterminds exist and he has bought none himself.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Oliver Brocato explains how he turned a viral-validated novelty product (sex chocolate) into an $11M/year brand with no outside funding. He covers picking a product that triggers emotion, building a brand instead of dropshipping, sourcing small manufacturers, and running hundreds of native-looking short-form videos a day through paid creators and repost accounts.

chunks.heading: Selling one product: Tabs Chocolate and the $11M/year model
chunks.text:
- Oliver sells "sex chocolate" online (Tabs Chocolate). It is an edible for sex that turns the most popular and effective natural supplements, which normally come as a pill or powder, into a high-end, luxurious experience.
- He expects about $11M in revenue for the year, with no outside investment. He reinvests every dollar into growth.
- He started it as a college freshman during a two-month winter break, and was a millionaire two years later at age 21.
- In the first year alone, Tabs was out of stock for more months than it had stock and still did about $4M.
- In the first three weeks he sold out of all inventory. In the first month he moved to pre-order and did over $280,000 in revenue at roughly 50% net margins.

chunks.heading: How he picked the product: spotting a viral loophole
chunks.text:
- A friend sent him a TikTok of a teenage girl reviewing a sex chocolate. It had 8 million views and 2 million likes, and the product had no website, Instagram or TikTok page.
- He took that as proof the concept could go viral, and decided his prior experience in this space could turn it into a multi-million dollar brand.
- Criteria he used: pick a product that "intrinsically goes viral". Tabs is novel, so people who have never seen it react.
- Key principle: virality runs on emotional arousal. Make the viewer feel a super intense emotion (the type doesn't matter). That makes people watch to the end and share with friends.
- He then spent a year building it "the right way", agonizing over every detail of the customer experience.

chunks.heading: Startup costs and finding a manufacturer
chunks.text:
- He started Tabs with $30,000, drained from his bank account, money earned from earlier ventures from when he was younger.
- He thinks almost any e-commerce brand can launch an MVP for about $10K. The biggest cost is R&D, then developing the first sample.
- Many manufacturers won't give a tiny brand the time of day. The goal is a small manufacturer willing to take you under its wing, which can get you under $10K.
- How he found one: he typed "chocolate contract manufacturer" into Google and went through the first 20 to 25 pages of results. He built a spreadsheet of each company's name, website and contact info, then phoned and emailed them.
- Supply chain: he designed the raw box files himself in Canva and Figma, then had a professional designer clean them up and get 3D renders made. The boxes are made in China. The chocolate, and everything that touches it, is made in the US, which he says is "super super important" to him.
- Each supplement has its own independent manufacturer because he sources the best of the best. Each chocolate also has its own wrapper manufacturer, and the chocolate is stamped with the logo and has a clean break line so it can be split.
- It took a year from idea to reality. He admits there were weeks he wasn't working on it because he was waiting on someone.

chunks.heading: Biggest operational mistake: inventory management
chunks.text:
- Inventory forecasting is his perpetual problem. After selling out, he shipped the next order of about 60,000 to 70,000 boxes by boat instead of air because it's much cheaper, but it takes four times as long.
- The container was delayed. He moved to pre-orders, sales declined to almost zero, and he calls it a disaster.
- His fix is to order as much inventory as he can, which is why he reinvests every dollar into boxes and chocolate.

chunks.heading: Why a brand beats dropshipping
chunks.text:
- He argues dropshipping "sucks" for most people. You sell a trendy product in a saturated market with no competitive advantage, so there's no reason for a buyer to choose you over Amazon or 150 other sellers. In his view the people making money from it are those selling courses.
- The power of a brand: you drop a product and it sells out in 30 seconds. You build a community and an identity where customers "live and breathe" your product.
- A cult-like following gives you evergreen customers who come back for new drops and new SKUs, so you can keep making money from the same cohort.
- Brand equity matters for the exit. He says real money is made on the exit, not on cash flow or yearly sales. Dropshipping has no equity, because you keep shutting down and opening new shops every couple of months.
- Takeaway: people thinking long term and building brands always win.

chunks.heading: The marketing engine: a UGC content machine
chunks.text:
- Most of his business comes from short-form social: TikTok, Instagram, YouTube and any other short-form platform. He says he has pushed out hundreds of millions of views on TikTok.
- He pays 60+ creators, and thousands of people repost the content across a web of accounts. Hundreds of videos go out every day, reaching millions of people and driving tens to hundreds of thousands of dollars in sales a day.
- Videos are made to look as native as possible. "Consumers are smart. If they think it's an ad, they're not going to watch it." Creators follow whatever is trending: the popping sound, the current movement or format. They also push some validated concepts that perform hard.
- It is mostly organic, with little paid advertising. He does "double down" by taking his best-performing creatives and paying meme pages with tens of millions of followers to post them.
- Other channels: a little Google Ads, plus email and text message marketing, which he calls bottom of the funnel.
- He credits this organic system, which he says he pioneered, for the $11M+ year.

chunks.heading: Advice for starting a brand
chunks.text:
- "I'm not smarter than you. I don't have a higher IQ." There is no gatekept secret sauce: go make it happen and never look back.
- Progress compounds daily, and in 3, 5 or 10 years people won't recognize how far you've come.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Oliver Brocato explains the three organic pillars (content creators, meme pages, influencers) behind his $10M revenue with zero paid ads. The core engine is a high-volume TikTok content studio of many creators on rev-share, using a controversy post plus reply-to-comment sales videos, then repurposing via affiliates.

chunks.heading: Oliver's organic growth model: three distribution pillars
chunks.text:
- Oliver says he is 21, expects about $10 million in revenue this year, and did over 500 million views in 2022. He expects to exceed 1 billion this year, with no paid ads.
- He credits an organic strategy for most of his success: "three pillars". These are content creators, memes and influencers.
- The goal is reach, website visitors and sales without paying Facebook or running pay-per-click.
- He cites peers using TikTok organically: a slime brand doing more than $20 million in sales, and a brand called Mini Katanas that sells swords through TikTok.

chunks.heading: TikTok: build a content studio, not one account
chunks.text:
- Oliver calls TikTok a "blue ocean": for the first time you can reach millions of people for little to no money. He uses it as top-of-funnel brand awareness.
- He works with user-generated-content (UGC) creators, not big-follower influencers. Each creator gets a brand-owned account on which they are the "Mastermind" with free rein.
- Once one creator works, he repeats it with more creators from different backgrounds and angles. The aim is "a content studio with 400 different creators on your retainer", not one TikTok page.
- His reasoning: "no one can tell you what video is going to go viral", so the only way to win is scale.
- His examples include accounts run by a grandma, a college kid and a prankster. He compares himself to a news channel: he doesn't try to pick the needle, he grabs "the whole entire haystack".
- Formula: quantity × quality = success. He says most people over-focus on quality. If you've made fewer than 500 videos, you haven't given organic TikTok a fair shot.
- Quality should come from the creators, not the founder. Don't micromanage with scripts. Hire talent, cut low performers and double down on people who produce views.
- Account names don't matter. He runs several differently named brand accounts and says viewers don't remember them, and TikTok's base is over a billion users. If an account gets banned or shadow-banned, he makes a new one, and says a fresh account can even perform better early on.

chunks.heading: Creator pay structure: small retainer plus 20% affiliate
chunks.text:
- He hires as many creators as he can on a recurring model, not one-post deals.
- Pay is a hybrid: a very small base retainer plus a large affiliate share, 20% of all sales the creator generates.
- Reason: it aligns incentives. If pay isn't tied to performance, a creator can drive 2 million views and only $100 in sales with no reason to care.
- Principle: "pay out as little money as possible and as big of a rep share as you can afford. When they win you win."

chunks.heading: The one-two punch: viral video, then reply videos that sell
chunks.text:
- Punch one: make a controversial or attention-grabbing video that isn't about selling or converting. The goal is eyeballs and top-of-funnel awareness.
- Punch two: once a video is viral, make videos replying to comments on it. You can make as many reply videos as you want.
- Reply videos are where you "sell hard". List features, benefits and value propositions, say what separates you from competitors, and address friction points and pain points.
- If there aren't enough valid comments, he says to create comments about the points you want to address.

chunks.heading: Sourcing creators and recycling content through affiliates
chunks.text:
- Finding creators: search Twitter and LinkedIn for "UGC", "user generated content", "UGC creator" and "TikTok content creator". Also use your own network, and DM people whose content you like while scrolling.
- Creators with under 5,000 followers tend to be more excited to work with you.
- Reposting: Oliver has more than 2,000 affiliates in a Discord, each with their own Instagram and YouTube accounts. They repost his most viral videos as Reels and Shorts across hundreds or thousands of accounts. Some posts hit about 1-5 million views, and reposters are paid on affiliate commission too.

chunks.heading: Meme pages: rent distribution by the day
chunks.text:
- Pillar two is meme and theme pages on Instagram.
- He pays page owners $100, $300 or $500 for a 24-hour post. Owners change the link in their bio to his website for 24 hours.
- He turns his viral content into memes for this. The meme account's owned audience replaces paying Facebook or pay-per-click for traffic.

chunks.heading: Micro influencers: pay for distribution, work at scale
chunks.text:
- Pillar three is influencers, and he prefers micro influencers with roughly 20,000 to 200,000 followers. He wants their distribution network and content that might hit the For You page, not their brand name or status.
- Difficulties he lists: many ignore cold emails and DMs, many demand unaffordable deal structures, and some take the product and disappear. So you have to cast a wide net.
- Rules:
  - Scale is everything. He says to work with 300 influencers, not three: "you worked with three influencers... work with 300".
  - Don't go through an agency or manager, because you'll get ripped off and it won't be profitable.
  - Don't script it. Creators know how to speak to their audience. Only after they show a finished video should you tweak it so it converts as well as gets views.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Oliver Brocato recounts taking a single-product chocolate brand from zero to $3M in year one, then through a stockout, bans and a co-founder exit. Key lessons: pick products by marketability, replace one-off influencers with retained creators on dedicated accounts, and invest in packaging and team.

chunks.heading: Building a $10M-run-rate Shopify chocolate brand (TABS): the origin and product
chunks.text:
- Oliver went from zero to about $3M in revenue in the first year selling one product. By the time of the video he had about $2M year to date and an $8-10M run rate for the coming year.
- He says he is "no different" from the audience: not smarter, no higher IQ, he "just put in the work."
- The idea came from his partner, who found a TikTok about a sex chocolate with about 8 million views and 2 million likes. The brand had no social media and no website. Oliver saw large potential because marketing was his skill set.
- His view: "it really wasn't too much about the product but more so the potential to market it."
- Development took about a year to build the supply chain and formulation. They did not reinvent anything: they took popular, effective natural supplements that usually come as pills or powders and turned them into a luxury chocolate experience that tastes good.
- Contrast with gas-station pills, which people are afraid to talk about or admit to using. TABS flips that by being openly branded and giftable.
- Branding and packaging are what acquire customers; taste is what brings them back ("if the chocolate isn't good... they're never going to come back").
- Product details: a chocolatier and food scientist balanced efficacy with taste, and the chocolate uses a custom polycarbonate virgin mold for its shape.
- He stresses an operator has to own every detail: photography, website design and development, marketing, customer support.

chunks.heading: From influencer collabs to a retainer-based creator model
chunks.text:
- Launch was December 20, 2021. They sold out of inventory in the first three weeks.
- The influencer-driven strategy was not sustainable: each influencer post spiked sales, then sales fell back to near zero.
- Problems with influencer sourcing:
  - Hard to scale: of every 1,000 outreach emails, only 10-20 responded.
  - About 90% of responders asked exorbitant rates that were not profitable.
  - Of those who accepted, about half took the product and ghosted.
  - So a huge outreach net was needed to land a single working influencer.
- The switch: hire content creators on retainer instead of doing influencer collabs.
  - His first creator was paid a flat fee to make one TikTok a day for 30 days. That creator became one of his best friends.
  - That first 30 days generated roughly $60-80K in sales.
- Scaling it: rather than putting many creators on one account, he created new accounts and gave each creator their own independent account, hiring talented creators to run them.
- Core insight: "TikTok democratized the ability to go viral." It is about whether you can make content that hits the For You page, not follower count. You no longer pay someone a large amount to access their audience.
- Result: nearly all marketing for the first year to year and a half was 100% organic, with almost no paid ads (early ad accounts got banned within minutes).

chunks.heading: Viral spikes, the stockout mistake, and losing momentum
chunks.text:
- On January 15, 2022, a creator (Mossy Wolf) posted a TikTok about TABS that got over 6.6M views and over 2M likes in one day. That video drove over $50K in revenue.
- Month two revenue was about $280K, much of it pre-orders.
- The fatal mistake: the chocolate was made in the US but the packaging was made in China. To save money they shipped a full container by boat instead of air-freighting the packaging.
- The container was badly delayed and they were out of product for about three months. They lost all momentum and sales slowly declined.
- They restocked in April. Oliver assumed he could resume at the prior level, and says that was a mistake. His lesson: "this is a game of momentum."
- Takeaways he draws: do not trade supply-chain reliability for freight savings on a one-product brand, and momentum from virality is hard to regain once inventory runs out.

chunks.heading: The 40% revenue drop and the rebuild
chunks.text:
- After the stockout he moved to Miami and went all-in on the business, then in August revenue dropped 40% when TikTok started banning all their accounts and videos. He thought it was "game over."
- At the same time his co-founder disappeared and went back to school despite their pledge to take a gap year together. Oliver moved back home, which he calls one of the hardest moments of his life.
- What turned it around:
  - He rebuilt his health habits: eating clean, going to the gym, running.
  - He decided he had to build a real team instead of operating alone.
  - He hired help for email and SMS, conversion rate optimization (CRO) and creatives.
  - That setup went into Q4 holiday season, Black Friday and Cyber Monday, and sales "started to really take form and started to explode."
- His view on mindset: people say go into monk mode and hustle, but "if you're not happy with life... what is the point?" He says his well-being is tightly tied to business performance. He booked a one-way ticket to Europe and traveled, and says things improved across the board afterward.

chunks.heading: Team and channels that drove the $2M year
chunks.text:
- Oliver credits a "team of Assassins" as the reason TABS is successful.
- After the rebuild they started spending hundreds of thousands of dollars on:
  - Instagram memes and Twitter memes
  - Bigger influencers
  - Revamping the creator and influencer operation
  - Photo shoots
  - A full site redesign
  - A conversion rate optimization team
- He describes the result as taking off "like a rocket ship": about $2M year to date and an $8-10M run rate.

chunks.heading: Growth plan: international, new channels, paid ads, product extensions
chunks.text:
Three goals Oliver lays out for the coming months:

1. **Go international.** More than 40% of site traffic comes from outside the US, but TABS only sells domestically.
2. **Diversify beyond the DTC site.**
   - Amazon and Etsy.
   - Wholesale and retail: smoke shops, sex stores, convenience stores, gas stations.
   - Break into paid advertising, since nearly all marketing so far was organic.
3. **Build new product lines and extensions.** TABS is a one-product brand (a dark chocolate sex chocolate), so he wants new flavors, new "moods" and new products. His stated ambition is for it to be "the one-stop shop" in the category.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Oliver walks through his path from age 14 to 21: fidget spinners, a social media agency, failed dropshipping and Etsy chargebacks, consulting for a Blazer brand, TikTok influencer growth, and a viral leggings brand. Each stage built a skill (distribution, attribution, paid ads, influencer buying) that set up his chocolate brand.

chunks.heading: From fidget spinners to a viral TikTok leggings brand: Oliver's path, 14 to 18
chunks.text:
- At 14, Oliver saw fidget spinners take over his school and borrowed $500 from his grandpa as seed money. He bought a 3D printer, a rubber mallet and skateboard bearings.
- He printed frames after school and soaked the bearings in acetone to strip the grease, which gave longer spin times. He sold to classmates and built a commission-based team of friends who sold for him.
