- When spinners got banned at school, he sold door-to-door to business owners (20 or 50 at a time). A party planner then had him set up booths at bar mitzvahs and sweet 16s where kids printed and customized their own spinners. That made over $2,500 a night until he saturated the in-person market.
- He moved to eBay, ran keyword research and internal ads, and started an Instagram page to push external traffic to his listings. He sold over $50,000 of spinners by age 14. As he puts it, "as quick as the fidget spinner trend came they left."

chunks.heading: The social media agency lesson: no attribution means no impact
chunks.text:
- After spinners, Oliver started a social media agency called Star Social. His first clients were his barbers, who gave him free monthly haircuts in exchange for running their accounts, plus a room in the back of the shop.
- That led to referrals to the fish market, a clothing store and other local businesses. To deliver, he built a team: a photographer, a content strategist, a copywriter and a Philippines-based virtual assistant.
- Oliver's problem with pure social media management was attribution. There is no tracking of what the work actually does, so impact is impossible to prove.
- He concluded that paid ads (PPC) fix this because every event is measured. If he could drive real revenue for a store or brand owner, he "would be untouchable." That is why he set out to learn paid ads at 16.

chunks.heading: Failed experiments: dropshipping and the Etsy chargeback collapse
chunks.text:
- To learn paid ads, Oliver ran eight or nine dropshipping stores (charging cables, gadgets, kitchen supplies). He found no success. He says it is "certainly not a scam," but it wasn't for him.
- He went back to eBay and Etsy selling phone cases and wallets with no inventory and no costs, and became obsessed with growth-hacking listings to the top page and using each platform's native ad tools. He hit his first $1,000, $3,000 and $5,000 days.
- Then chargebacks hit: 30 or 40 at once. His supplier said they were shipping, but they were lying. He refunded close to 1,000 customers and lost every dollar he had made.
- The lesson he draws is implicit: a business that depends on a supplier you do not control can wipe out your gains overnight.

chunks.heading: Turning a $400/day Blazer store into $3,000/day
chunks.text:
- At 17, a friend (Jesse) asked Oliver to help his mom Andrea's fashion e-commerce business. Her wholesale and retail business was solid, but her website was broken English, had incomprehensible emails and was a mess. It still sold about one blazer a day, roughly $400 a day.
- Oliver says he knew he could turn it around. In the first month sales went from $400 a day to $3,000 a day. He says the changes were "super basic optimizations" plus a revamp, not anything exotic.
- When a reality TV star wore one of her blazers on TV, the next day did over $28,000 in sales.
- Andrea then let him go because she wanted a "professional agency," and told him she couldn't pay him more because "you're a kid." Her store manager earned more than he did. A year later she called to say she had been through countless agencies and was still using the flows he set up.
- Oliver says the skills from that job are a big part of why he is where he is today.

chunks.heading: Early TikTok influencer arbitrage at the "It's Me" app
chunks.text:
- At 17, a mentor (a few years older, heading up growth at the "It's Me" app, a 3D-avatar chat app backed by $15 million from the Reddit co-founder) brought Oliver in to pioneer TikTok influencer collaborations.
- Oliver explains why early TikTok was ripe for advertisers:
  - Influencers had never monetized on TikTok, so brand deals cost "pennies on the dollar."
  - Viewers had not seen ads on the platform, so they were more impressionable and more likely to convert. Today they scroll past ads, so there is more friction.
- He built a team of five Philippines-based virtual assistants. Two did list building: scraping TikTok for US-based creators with 50,000 to 500,000 followers.
- His logic on creator size: creators in that range don't charge big-name rates, so you pay for distribution rather than brand. Also, TikTok had democratized virality, so content mattered more than follower count.
- The app reached number four on the social networking chart, behind Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp.
- He was paid about $3,500 a month. The company, pressured to show astronomical growth before a fundraise, replaced him with an influencer agency costing $45,000 a month. "Money wasn't a problem for them... the only thing they cared about was showing growth."

chunks.heading: Scaling a viral TikTok leggings brand and deciding to start his own
chunks.text:
- At 18 (end of senior year, accepted to the University of Michigan Ross School of Business), Oliver was introduced to Jake, a 17-year-old dropshipping whiz, and Nico, an investor who had backed him. Jake and Nico hired Oliver to run their whole influencer collaboration process and he came on as an operator, effectively CEO.
- Together they sold over $1 million of viral TikTok leggings in about a year. Jake and Nico treated him as a partner, and he and Jake would talk for five hours at a time.
- The brand sold for mid six figures.
- Oliver says that by then he had the experience and intuition to know "exactly what I need to do to go from zero to five million," and so started his own brand, Types Chocolate.
- The frame he uses for the whole story: each venture, successful or not, built a skill that fed the next. Those skills included product sourcing, marketplace growth, paid ads, influencer sourcing, building teams of virtual assistants, and attribution thinking.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Oliver Brocato explains how Tabs did about $9M at a 40% net margin using only organic short-form video. He covers building a product primed for virality, running hundreds of creator-owned TikTok accounts on a hybrid retainer plus revenue-share deal, and recycling winners through meme pages and a Discord of reposters.

chunks.heading: How Oliver builds a no-ad organic marketing engine on short-form video
chunks.text:
- Oliver co-founded Tabs Chocolate. He says it did about $9 million in revenue last year at a 40% net profit margin, entirely from organic strategies with no paid ads (Meta and TikTok ads are blocked in his sex/supplement category).
- The product is aphrodisiac chocolate with natural supplements (maca, epimedium, DHEA) that normally come as pills or powder. He turned a taboo into a "shared luxury experience."
- He started in e-commerce at 14 with fidget spinners. He later co-founded a leggings brand that grew 0 to 7 figures on early TikTok with micro-influencers, then got squeezed out because it had no patents, IP or ownership. "We simply slapped our logo on it."
- For the next product he set two requirements: inherently viral and engineered for TikTok, and a space with high barriers to entry so nobody can dupe it from an AliExpress supplier.
- He found the idea in a random TikTok about a competing aphrodisiac chocolate with 7 million views and 2 million likes. The competitor had no website, no social presence and terrible branding and packaging. He built a premium, camera-friendly version: each square sits in a divot with emojis underneath, and the bar breaks in half, one half per partner.

chunks.heading: Build virality into the product first
chunks.text:
- His rule: nothing else works unless the product itself is built and primed for virality.
- A viral product needs to be edgy and a scroll-stopper. It can't be a commoditized good you'd find at a mom-and-pop shop, on Amazon or at Target. It has to be novel.
- Examples he cites:
  - Cloudy Vapes: a melatonin diffuser, like a vape without nicotine. It takes something people know and adds a twist.
  - Mini Katana: tiny anime swords, eight figures a year, all from their own TikTok channel.
  - Peachy: slime, a category already satisfying and big in short form. The founder is on track for over $25 million this year, has never run a paid Facebook ad, and just launched his first email and SMS campaign.

chunks.heading: Why influencer outreach failed and horizontal scaling worked
chunks.text:
- Early micro-influencer outreach was a logistical mess:
  - Instagram rate-limited DMs.
  - Influencers ghosted or charged "an arm and a leg."
  - Spreadsheets, VAs and agencies didn't fix it.
  - Sales were a roller coaster: one influencer video drove $500 to $1,000 in a day, then sales returned to zero.
- His conclusion: "if we put out enough short form we will inevitably win," so the job is systemizing output.
- He found a dropshipper called Key via a tweet, who promoted high-powered flashlights only through a TikTok brand page posting 1 to 3 videos a day. Key had a $30,000 sales day.
- Oliver pitched him: stay in your zone of genius, make high-converting viral content, and be an affiliate for Tabs while Oliver handles e-commerce. Key posted over 90 videos in month one and drove $8,000 in revenue.
- That revealed a whole community of creators like Key on Twitter/X. Oliver onboarded them the same way, each with their own independent TikTok account, and scaled horizontally to hundreds of creators and hundreds of accounts.
- His reasons for one account per creator:
  - TikTok favors accounts that follow a specific formula and style. Many creators on one page means "too many cooks" and TikTok stifles views.
  - Separate accounts give clean analytics on who drives views and sales, which matters when paying on performance.
  - It plays the law of averages and large numbers.
  - Diverse creators bring diverse audiences: young creators get shown to young people, an LGBTQ creator to LGBTQ audiences. Each account acts like a miniature ad set.
- Follower count barely matters on TikTok; video quality does. He points out Charli D'Amelio has a secondary account with a default avatar and a random username that still gets huge views.
- He is explicit that this is a "spray and pray" model: work with many creators, expect most to ghost or make weak content, and operate at enough scale to see returns. His minimum test is 3 to 5 creators for 3 months. Judging after half a month is like loading Facebook ads or Amazon PPC with an absurdly low budget and being disappointed.

chunks.heading: Finding, paying and onboarding creators
chunks.text:
**Who to recruit**
- He doesn't want "pretty UGC types" with nice-looking videos. He wants people whose videos convert and drive traffic and sales.
- His niche is dropshippers who already promote their own stores through organic TikTok. He found most creators by building in public on Twitter, posting "we're hiring" tweets with a Google Form link, and onboarding "anybody and everybody."
- On fear that creators will steal the account: he says it won't happen, and worst case a contract protects you.

**Pay structure (hybrid)**
- Keep upfront cash as low as possible, but creators need to eat, so he pays a retainer of about $500 to $1,000 a month plus 20% of revenue they drive.
- The 20% applies only to attributed revenue (UTM link or promo code). Most sales aren't tracked that way, since people see a video and search the brand organically, so he says the true cost is more like 4% to 10% of revenue.
- Tools he recommends: Exolyt for analytics; Social Snowball for UTM links, promo codes and paying creators at scale.

**Onboarding**
- Give a very general brief (good lighting, broad basics).
- Give a document of past viral videos rather than scripts. "What goes viral once will go viral again," especially with a twist or a different face.
- Give creative control and freedom. He hires talent and lets them run. The only asks are one TikTok a day and consistency.
- Communicate by iMessage, not Discord or Slack. Creators are part-time people with other jobs and brands. His VA texts every creator each morning ("good morning, we're excited for you, send us a link once it's live").
- Build community: monthly Google Meet or Zoom with bonuses for most-viewed, best-performing and funniest video. When a video goes viral, it's sent to everyone and everyone remakes it, so information isn't siloed.

chunks.heading: The "one-two hook" content strategy
chunks.text:
- **Hook one:** every video is optimized for virality and brand awareness. It's general, not an in-depth product pitch, and the product appears but isn't the headline. The goal is as many eyeballs as possible. Early on he borrowed concepts from competitors and tangential spaces, since things that went viral will go viral again.
- **Hook two:** once a video hits, make follow-up videos that reply to comments on it. This uses TikTok's reply-to-comment-with-video feature, which puts the comment in the new video. TikTok retargets viewers of the original viral video. These follow-ups push the product, the website, FOMO/urgency and objection handling.
- All creators shoot for virality first, then convert that attention.
- Example winning format from Key: "finding Tabs in my Airbnb." It was milked with other creators ("finding Tabs in my sister's boyfriend's room," "in the school parking lot"), then new angles were needed as it saturated. Oliver says the creative innovation came from creators; his role is building the systems to bring on more of them.
- He doesn't point creators to the website in the video itself. Brand and product mention is enough in hook one.
- Team: a lean, contractor-based team. An operations lead handles day-to-day, VAs check in, and nothing is full-time. Agencies or specialists handle Instagram meme media buying, email, conversion rate optimization and Google ads.
- If TikTok Shop were available to him, he'd bolt it on, since TikTok is heavily pushing shop-enabled videos (some creators list a 99-cent product to game it). He can't use it because of his category's restrictions.
- Alternative to spray-and-shoot: focus on one channel with a full-time person. He names Midday Squares (a TV-show-style behind-the-scenes account) and Mini Katana (high-production stunts, like catching a bullet with a sword). He prefers spray-and-shoot because it mitigates risk when pages in his space get banned or shadowbanned often, but says to evaluate both.

chunks.heading: Giving winning content a second life: meme pages
chunks.text:
- He takes his most validated TikTok creatives, shrinks them onto a white background, adds a caption, and pays Instagram and Twitter meme pages to post them.
- Theme networks reach hundreds of millions of followers and billions of impressions a month. Proven-viral content plus built-in distribution gives another viral round with no new production.
- You need an inside man or agency with direct relationships, because the space is run by 16- to 22-year-olds in Telegram groups. His media buyers run their own pages of roughly 3 to 4 million followers.

chunks.heading: Syndicating content with a Discord of reposters
chunks.text:
- His rule: if it went viral on TikTok, it will likely go viral on Instagram Reels, Facebook Reels, YouTube Shorts and Pinterest idea pins.
- First attempt: a VA opened about 10 accounts per platform and posted manually. He also tried Repurpose.io. It worked somewhat but didn't hit the scale he wanted. "I didn't want to put 10 reposts a day up, I wanted to put 10,000."
- He built a Discord of kids who want to make money online. He coaches them to open pages with names like "tabs chocolate 1" or "the viral chocolates," gives them photos and captions for the feed plus the viral creative library, and asks for one short-form post a day.
- Results to date: over 7,000 members, over $172,000 paid out, and viral reposts at 11 million, 9 million and 7 million views.
- Pay: a percentage of revenue they drive, tracked via UTM link and promo code in Social Snowball.
- Gamification:
  - Daily: everyone who posts and reacts goes on a wheel, and five random people win money.
  - 30 straight days of posting unlocks a salary.
  - A community feel, including a gym channel where members share progress selfies.
- He originally wanted members to make original content but says it was too big an ask. Reposts of proven viral videos outperformed their own mediocre content.

chunks.heading: Reusing the content flywheel elsewhere
chunks.text:
- The constant stream of content can be clipped into compilations for the website, email and SMS.
- He says you should "never pay a UGC creator again" to make ads, since you already have the footage for paid ads.
- He sees a big opportunity on Amazon. On Shopify you must keep hitting view counts monthly to sustain sales, but on Amazon a product that blows up from this strategy can reach page one or two and get evergreen sales from Amazon's algorithm. He cites a friend, Robert Oliver, doing this and crushing it.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Oliver tells his story from fidget spinners to a multi-million chocolate brand, a near-collapse in July 2022, and what he learned. Core lessons: define goals, stack reps, build a personal brand on Twitter for team and network, and share unfiltered stories. Light on tactics, strong on mindset.

chunks.heading: Oliver's origin: the fidget spinner hustle and early reps
chunks.text:
- Oliver traces his entrepreneurship to a natural drive: in third grade he ran "pencil insurance," where kids paid one pencil a week and he replaced any lost pencil free. He had commission-based recruiters negotiating deals with other classes and kept the pencils in a fake tissue box, treating them as social currency.
- Around age 14 in 2016 he saw a senior (Alan) put fidget spinners on the map at their school. His reaction: "what does he have that I don't have? I could make these, I could sell these too."
- He built spinners with a donated 3D printer, sold to classmates, then expanded in layers: door-knocking local stores for wholesale, bar mitzvahs and events (3D printers on site, paid by the sponsor), and custom spinners with company logos as recruiting swag.
- When the local market saturated, he moved online to eBay and Etsy. Because he was early in the trend, he optimized listings, copied competitors' keywords, used the best photography, and put an insert in each order offering money off for positive reviews. His listing ranked at the top when people searched "fidget spinner."
- He says that opened him to e-commerce and he "hasn't looked back."
- Other early reps: a social media agency at 15 running Instagram accounts for local mom and pop shops. His first client, his barber, paid in a free haircut. He describes "scores of mini businesses," most of them failures, each adding wisdom.

chunks.heading: Compounding reps, pattern recognition and why business gets easier
chunks.text:
- Oliver's view: success comes from experience and intuition rather than IQ. Each failed project is a rep that improves you "by 0.1 percent," and compounding makes success eventually inevitable.
- He compares it to machine learning: after enough situations you recognize which moves work, while newcomers "step on the landmine."
- Reps are also the "universal currency of respect." Doing 400 podcast episodes or 50 business iterations signals seriousness.
- Time in the game is the biggest competitive advantage. He says he spent seven years in the game before Tabs, with many failures.
- Concrete example of it getting easier: with a new SaaS tool (Study Buddy) he went from zero to 2,000 subscribers and $25,000 MRR in two weeks, profitably. He says he had a blueprint: the email flows, the ad types and creatives, the team and the Rolodex of contacts.
- Later-stage advantages he lists:
  - Network alpha: eight-figure operators share information in group chats, Discord and Slack, so he knew about a Facebook update a month early.
  - A Facebook ad rep he can call, instead of having no idea what to do if ads break.
  - Self-funding, so he can hire employees and agencies he once only dreamed of.
  - Lower fear of loss: losing $5-20K used to mean game over, and now a failed business just means starting a new one.
- His caution: he still has levels above him ("some people know how to take it from zero to one billion").

chunks.heading: Tabs chocolate: scale and numbers
chunks.text:
- Oliver founded Tabs, a chocolate brand. In its first month it did $280,000 in revenue, sold out of all inventory in the first three weeks, then went viral and took a wave of pre-orders.
- He says the company hit $11 million in a year at 40-45% margins, and that he was 21 and a multimillionaire at the time of recording (May 2023).
- He first paid himself in January 2023, about two and a half years in. Before that he reinvested every dollar into inventory and growth, because inventory is what keeps growth going. He recounts being unable to afford an Uber to a Miami boat day or lunch while giving a talk to a design agency.
- He kept his relationship with money: he still values a dollar the same way and does not spend crazily.
- In July 2022 the business hit a wall: sales fell about 60% in one month and the brand was banned on every social platform. In the same stretch his co-founder said he was going back to school and doing the minimum for his contractual obligations, one intern-turned-roommate left, and another employee tried to extort equity. He was alone in an unfurnished Miami apartment he could not really afford and could not re-enroll in school for a year.
- He recovered by moving back to his parents' house and slowly rebuilding. He says there was no single switch or trick, just time.

chunks.heading: Twitter as a distribution and network engine
chunks.text:
- Oliver started tweeting around September 2019 with zero followers and got nothing for a long time. It took off when he began documenting building Tabs: behind the scenes, tactics, strategy and the reasoning behind decisions, "unfiltered" and including the good, bad and ugly.
- He has about 21,000 followers and argues that is more powerful than a 3 million follower Instagram account because the audience is entrepreneurs, mostly in e-commerce, many running multi-million dollar businesses.
- What it produced:
  - Most of his team came directly from Twitter or indirectly through friends there who recommended people.
  - Mentors, advisors and friendships far beyond his geography. He compares it to being "confined geographically" before, with friends chosen by convenience in a two-mile radius.
  - Access: tweeting "I'm in X city, who wants to grab a coffee" gets him hosts, gym passes and stays. He says "anything is one tweet away" and calls it living life on easy mode.
- His YouTube channel (around 3,000 subscribers at recording) is not about direct revenue. He sells no course or Discord and says he spends roughly $5,000 a month on an editor, thumbnails, equipment and travel, with no monetary ROI. He invests because of the life impact, and he sees personal brand and social currency as something to double down on.

chunks.heading: Mindset: define the goal, embody it, keep going
chunks.text:
- Oliver's core belief is self-confidence: he always felt "destined for more," and says he credits "the vast majority" of his success to it, since "if you don't believe it, how are you ever going to get there."
- On manifesting: he does not buy the spiritual version, but he does believe that if you define your goal, think about it and obsess over it, you will reach it, as long as you then execute. "Most people don't even know what they want."
- His origin of ambition: his best friend Jack's father left a normal career, bet on himself and became a hedge fund multimillionaire. Oliver saw that his own father was equally brilliant, and the only difference was that Jack's dad took the risk. Oliver says he vowed to bet on himself.
- He sees access to the top as more attainable than people assume ("anybody can do it if they want it bad enough"), though he acknowledges survivorship bias and that upbringing programmed him.
- On persistence he uses the woodpecker and boiling-point analogies: you can be 0.01 degrees from the boiling point with no visible movement, so you cannot quit.
- On starting: "The best time to have taken action was yesterday, the second best is now." The perfect moment does not exist, since college, parents, money or golden handcuffs will always give a reason to wait.
- His weekly takeaway challenge: take 60 seconds, close your eyes, define where you want to be in 5 and 10 years, write it down, and live it every waking moment by putting it on a mirror, laptop or phone screen.

chunks.heading: Staying motivated after success, and what money changes
chunks.text:
- Oliver says he thrives in chaos and pressure (he has ADHD). Once the business ran smoothly, with systems working and the team strong, he was bored and struggled to find his earlier hunger.
- He warns that it is easy to get addicted to "cheap dopamine" and coast, which brings its own misery.
- His answer was to move into new challenges: personal brand, YouTube, and a new software business (Study Buddy), though he notes that advisors usually say to focus on one thing.
- He says money does not change who you are, since "we all bleed the same blood" and have similar fears, but it gives tools, freedom and independence. It validated beliefs he held at 16, with a caveat that this partly reflects survivorship bias. It also swaps survival problems for existential ones.
- On motivation shifting: early on it was spite and a chip on his shoulder (rejected from top fraternities, doubted by family and peers). Now he says he has less to prove, and motivation comes from being in rooms with people "a hundred times farther ahead," which humbles him. Bigger watches and boats inspire him rather than upset him, because it shows the level is attainable.
- On money as a scoreboard: he is not optimizing for money but for growth, and money follows the impact and value created.
- On the cost of the path: remote team, no office, friends busy on their own paths, so entrepreneurship can feel lonely. He accepts it as a sacrifice that comes with the level he wants, and says he does not envy the college social life he left.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Oliver Brocato explains how Tabs Chocolate grew with no paid ads. He moved from one-off influencers to one-creator-per-account TikTok pages, then added a 2,000-person affiliate Discord. He also covers why experience compounds into intuition, why focus beats jumping between projects, and how a public build-in-public Twitter journey brings in inbound deals.

chunks.heading: How Oliver launched Tabs Chocolate and survived being banned from paid ads
chunks.text:
- Tabs Chocolate is an adult-product brand Oliver co-founded with Jake (50/50 partners). Oliver says it went from zero to seven figures "pretty much solely through organic."
- At launch the brand was banned from Facebook, TikTok ads, Google ads and Snapchat ads, so he was forced into alternative channels. He had TikTok in mind from the start.
- In the weeks before launch he worked around the clock messaging influencers through DMs, texts, the TikTok Creator Marketplace and email.
  - Criteria: US-based, 50k to 250k followers (micro creators, cheaper), plus a few based creators.
  - He landed roughly 20 to 30 in the pipeline.
- Result of the one-off posts: revenue spiked when an influencer posted (a few hundred dollars up to a couple thousand on a good one), then dropped back to zero the next day. He called it a good sign but not a baseline.
- He found one-off influencer work unsustainable. It took thousands of DMs, emails and texts. Most people ignore you, those who reply charge exorbitant rates, and half of those who say yes ghost after getting the product. He built a team of virtual assistants to run it and still called it "a crap shoot."

chunks.heading: The TikTok organic system: one creator per brand-page account
chunks.text:
- Oliver connected with Jimmy Farley and Kimiko, who were pioneering TikTok organic: create a brand-page account, put a creator on retainer, and have them post about 30 TikToks over a month (one a day).
- His first creator, Keon, did roughly $60-70k in sales in the first month, directly attributable to his account.
- Scaling problem: adding more creators to the same account hurts the algorithm. TikTok "doesn't want too many chefs in the kitchen." It understands an account's person, ethos and consistency, then shows good ones to an audience. Eight creators with eight styles lose the account's niche.
- Examples he gives of accounts that win by repeating one format: the Subway guy and the Coldstone ice cream account (Dylan Lemay), the same video over and over.
- His solution: scale horizontally. One independent creator per account, across many accounts. Over about eight months he scaled to 100+ creators and 100+ accounts.
- It is still one of Tabs' strongest channels and produces an "overwhelming" share of monthly revenue. It runs as a constant hamster wheel: bring in new creators, test them, cut low performers, double down on high performers. Many of the original creators have been cut over time.
- Oliver says he is not claiming to have invented the strategy but was an early pioneer, and notes someone else ran the astrology version of it better than he did.

chunks.heading: The affiliate Discord: 2,000 affiliates reposting content
chunks.text:
- Oliver runs a Discord with about 2,000 affiliates. They take Tabs' viral content and post it on their own subsidiary brand pages (Instagram, YouTube and more) with unique coupon codes.
- Everyone posts the same videos at different times and in different geographies, and randomly some hit 1 to 7 million views. Per-affiliate coupon codes make revenue attributable.
- He says it has generated over half a million dollars in revenue in roughly four months, directly from reposts.
- How he incentivizes it:
  - 20% commission on any sale.
  - A base-pay stipend for posting 30 days straight.
  - Daily raffle spins: a VA compiles the names of people who posted and reacted, spins a wheel, and the winner gets $5, with three or four spins a day.
  - Challenges, such as inviting the most people in a day wins $100.
  - A wins chat running 24/7 (first sale, $1,000 in commissions), plus general, gym and game chats so it feels like a community, not just a payout.
- He describes it as applying the Andrew Tate clipping model to an e-commerce brand and says he gamified the whole thing inside Discord.
- On attribution: he admits organic is hard to attribute, but says he lives and breathes the business and has a "Spider Sense" for what is pushing, from watching views and channels.

chunks.heading: What's next for Tabs: from seven to eight figures
chunks.text:
Oliver names three levers:
1. **International.** About 40% of all traffic comes from outside the US, and Tabs only ships domestically, so shipping internationally is a big unlock.
2. **More channels.** Currently fully direct-to-consumer on Shopify. He wants Amazon and Walmart, plus wholesale to mom-and-pop shops: smoke shops, sex shops, convenience stores, hotels, cruises.
3. **Paid ads.** He started with no connections; now if a Facebook account is banned he can call friends to get it live, or talk to a Facebook rep. They are testing Facebook and Google with a new landing page, PG-friendly ad creative and reframed copy.

Beyond that he will keep scaling existing systems and wants to return to his roots by working with bigger influencers at bigger spend. He also says Twitter theme pages are "super powerful, super slept on," but only work with a viral, edgy, eye-catching product. Tabs plays the game "on easy mode" in that sense.

chunks.heading: Advice: start with TikTok organic and stick to one thing
chunks.text:
- For people starting or stuck, Oliver says the biggest opportunity now is TikTok organic. You can test and validate a product for free, no creator needed.
  - He would post three TikToks a day, or be the face of the brand himself.
  - He cites founders telling stories and showing behind the scenes, so customers fall in love with the brand's ethos, "which is incredibly powerful because obviously you can sell them anything."
  - He thinks no other channel lets an entry-level person go from zero to six or seven figures with only time and hard work as investment.
- Intuition is the moat. He argues the person doing eight or nine figures is not smarter, just has "seen more." Experience leads to intuition leads to success. The same principles apply whether selling chocolate, leggings or software.
- Focus beats jumping around. The people who win do one thing "like a machine" over years and compound. He warns against drifting from day trading to NFTs to crypto to dropshipping.
- Start now: he points to Airbnb's ugly first site as proof that the key is starting and seeing it through.

chunks.heading: Building a personal brand and finding partners
chunks.text:
- Oliver has documented the Tabs journey on Twitter for about two years: behind-the-scenes, tactics, strategy, "sauce," plus thoughts and feelings.
- All his agency clients (G Fuel, with talks with Budweiser and Orangetheory) came inbound from that. The agency has no website, business card or logo.
- He spends roughly 30 to 60 minutes a day in DMs. He doesn't sell a course or run a Discord, and sees the return in friendships, connections, exchanged tactics and unexpected opportunities (even investor offers).
- He suggests a VA or appointment setter to triage DMs into a primary inbox and a general one.
- Plans: a YouTube channel, maybe a newsletter, and clipping long-form into TikTok.
- On partnerships: do exceptional work and people line up to work with you. "If you want to find a good partner you need to be a good partner yourself." Partnerships are like marriage, so get on a call, befriend the person and do some work first, rather than cold DMing a partnership pitch.
- His agency partnership with Jimmy came from both taking on clients on the side, then realizing the synergy. Jake came through a mutual contact and working together day in and day out.

chunks.heading: Operating habits, mindset and current projects
chunks.text:
- Current projects: Tabs is the main priority. He also runs a spin-off agency that applies the systems he built for Tabs to other brands (G Fuel and others), and is building a Shopify app (early stage, about eight months out, with a designer doing grunt work).
- He ended up part-time at the University of Michigan (Ross, business), then took a gap year. He did it gradually (full-time to part-time to a gap year, noting he could take up to 10) rather than dropping out at once.
- His family is corporate and high-achieving, so his parents initially pushed back, then came around. A text from his dad saying he was proud meant a lot to him.
- Routine: wakes around 6 to 6:30, goes to the gym right away (he says he has ADHD and exercise helps focus and productivity), is in bed around 9:30 to 10. He uses cold plunges and works with a fitness and life coach. He believes health, discipline and business are all tied together.
- On setbacks early on: the partner went missing, a right-hand guy tried to extort him for equity, TikTok banned every video, and he questioned leaving school. His view: the lower the lows, the more they recalibrate you, and every successful person has stories of getting scammed, going broke or nearly losing it all.
- He lives with fellow entrepreneurs Jimmy Farley and Luke in Scottsdale. He says surrounding yourself with people in the same trenches, who share strategies and compete, speeds up growth. He met them on Twitter and chose the location for the people, not the place.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Oliver Brocato, who exited Tabs Chocolate and now runs Bustem (anti-counterfeit takedowns for ecom brands), explains how he reuses a 50k-person audience as distribution, frames every message in dollars recovered, and prices with a performance model that upsells into an unlimited retainer. He also contrasts consumer and B2B growth.

chunks.heading: Oliver's path from DTC brand to B2B SaaS (Bustem)
chunks.text:
- Oliver started Taps Chocolate, scaled it from $30,000 of starting capital to an eight-figure-a-year business, and exited about two years before this conversation.
- He deliberately avoided another ecom brand. He was burnt out on "shilling" products and wanted something more product-focused and value-driven, where he could still use his strengths.
- He chose ecom SaaS because he was familiar with it (in ecom since age 14), knew the operators, and had a distribution edge. He compares the move to Peter Rahal building David after RXBAR: "that's compounding."
- He picked software over a course ("that would ruin my reputation") or an agency ("I don't know a single agency guy that likes what he does"). Software is infinitely scalable and carries the highest valuations.
- He built an audience of about 50,000 ecom entrepreneurs by building Taps in public. When he tweeted about an agency or software vendor, they got about 15 DMs overnight.
- Through affiliate partnerships with the vendors he used, his UTM links drove over $2 million in tracked deal flow. His conclusion: stop being a "street promoter" for other people's offers and build his own offer on his own distribution.

chunks.heading: What Bustem sells and how it prices
chunks.text:
- The product scans the internet for counterfeits, copycats, scammers and content thieves ripping off brands. Enforcement agents, mostly in South Africa, handle takedowns.
- Takedowns go through DMCA, cease and desists, reports to domains, registrars, hosting providers and payment processors, and payment blocks, avoiding court that "would take years and hundreds of thousands of dollars."
- He estimates brands bleed 5 to 15% of revenue to bad actors. He buckets it all together: counterfeits, competitors stealing content or ads and inflating CPMs, fake listings, duplicated sites, ads on branded keywords.
- Two pricing models:
  - Performance: $300/month platform fee plus $50 to $200 per successful takedown, billed only after the takedown lands.
  - Unlimited retainer: $2,500 to $5,000/month.
- The performance tier works as a natural upsell. Clients who see many bad actors do the math and ask to move to unlimited. One brand, Kill Crew, racked up 30 to 40 kills in nine days, then signed a 12-month contract at $3K/month about 10 days in.
- His analogy: "$20 a chicken finger or $30 for the whole buffet."
- Longer term, he wants to automate identification and enforcement and drop monitoring toward free as a lead magnet, then charge only per successful removal, with unlimited retainers for high-volume brands. He admits the tech is hard because it requires scrapers for platforms that don't want to be scraped.
- Small brands outnumber big ones roughly 10 to 1 at the door, so he splits focus between both.

chunks.heading: Making ROI the center of the product and sales
chunks.text:
- Founders get angry about copycats ("[ __ ] that guy"), but he says the emotion gets them on a call and the job is then to tie it to the P&L: "if you're not close to the P&L, you're [ __ ]."
- He frames everything as dollars: revenue lost per bad actor, revenue "recovered" per takedown. He admits the recovery number is a stretch, since takedown doesn't literally return the money.
- He wants to guarantee a 5x ROI, saying it improves retention and customer satisfaction.
- Credibility tactic: show the formula. Inputs are traffic times conversion rate times AOV, with sliders the brand can adjust, because "anybody could say that you're getting a 10x ROI."
- Put the dollar figure everywhere in the product:
  - Each bad-actor review card shows the money lost, with approve or deny buttons.
  - A running total across all cards sits at the top.
  - Per-client Slack channels get daily automations with takedown counts and estimated revenue.
  - A Slack alert fires at 15 bad actors pending review, for example "30 bad actors... potentially $30,000 a month."
  - Weekly and monthly reports lead with the dollar amount.
- He says ROI alone isn't enough; the product also has to be hard to replace. His competition is a VA with no technology, or a lawyer who bills what Bustem charges for a half-hour call.
- On putting prices on a website, he reported split testing it: "conversion rate took a massive dump when I put the pricing on the website."

chunks.heading: Distribution and growth tactics for Bustem
chunks.text:
- His main weapon is the audience from Taps. The launch tweet for Bustem got over 250,000 impressions and over 400 signups on day one.
- He posts daily and books three to five calls off his X account.
- He runs cold email framed around specific, hard-to-ignore proof:
  - "We found over 200 copycats and counterfeits that are ripping you off. Do you want to see the list?"
  - "I almost got scammed by a product pretending to be you guys... do you want to see the link?"
  - His reasoning: no one replies "no, I don't want to see the link."
- Referrals and word of mouth are the largest driver of clients; in SaaS, he argues, you're rewarded for building a good product.
- He notes distribution lessons from Taps still apply: understanding the Twitter algorithm, getting attention, and being scrappy. But the audience and playbooks are different, so in many ways he's "starting over."
- A SEO mistake: he bought bust.co to save about 5K, later bought bust.com, and a migration issue between the two domains means bust.com doesn't show up when searching "bust" on Google. He's working with an SEO agency and running Google ads on branded terms to catch warm intent.

chunks.heading: DTC versus B2B SaaS: how the games differ
chunks.text:
- DTC marketing is one-to-many and aimed at a huge audience. B2B is "hand-to-hand combat," with every deal involving decision makers, buy-in and calls where prospects "fall off a cliff."
- B2B inputs map to outputs more directly. He can calculate emails sent, reply rate, booked calls and close rate, so the outcome feels predictable and rewarding. Ecom felt less in his control, with big months coming from decisions made months earlier, platform timing (he was early on organic TikTok), or the right tailwind.
- Consumer, to him, is "all marketing," almost a content agency. He says it's about acquiring customers with a CAC lower than LTV. SaaS rewards focusing on product and retention, and he thinks focusing on product is better long term.
- In SaaS you play two games at once: the product game and the marketing and distribution game. In ecom, the product is fixed and you only market it, because iteration is slow (sell out inventory, change the formula, three-month lead time, two months shipping).
- SaaS is slow for a non-technical founder. He has a one-person dev shop, is hiring a second full-time engineer, and says everything "takes three or four times longer" than estimated, leaving him feeling two or three months behind the product in his head.
- He sees continuous iteration as an upside: churn, onboarding and retention are levers to pull, so improving the product can drive growth without acquiring more customers.

chunks.heading: Retention and upgrades via product design
chunks.text:
- The review-card UI makes the value of each takedown visible, which pushes customers up the pricing ladder from per-kill to unlimited.
- Customers on the performance model with no minimum rarely pause, since $300/month is cheap "insurance" for 24/7 monitoring, daily scans and manual enforcement sweeps.
- He currently runs a hybrid of software and agency, with human enforcement agents, and plans to phase them out as automation improves.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Oliver explains why building in public increases "surface area for luck," then lays out his 2024 plan: scale his personal brand (over $40k/month) into a media company and push his AI study tool from about $25k to $250k MRR. He is candid about being stuck on paid acquisition and the persistence mindset he's using to push through the plateau.

chunks.heading: Why Oliver builds in public and how he thinks about a personal brand
chunks.text:
- Oliver separates himself from the "get rich" content crowd. He says people pumping videos like "how to make your first $10,000" are running a content business: ad revenue, sponsorships, affiliate deals, or selling a course.
- He states he is "not a content creator" or an influencer, has "no stake in this game," and is not trying to make money off his audience. He frames his content as chronicling what he's doing and showing what's possible.
- He admits it is partly selfish. He started building in public 3 years ago with his e-commerce brand Tops, and says it changed his life through the people, advisers, investors, friends and network it opened up.
- Example of the payoff: he can tweet "I need a Google ads guy," "my Facebook ad account got banned," or "if anybody knows a good designer hit me up" and within seconds has scores of messages from people offering to help.
- His principle: "by establishing a personal brand you increase your surface area for luck and opportunity like nothing else."

chunks.heading: His 2024 situation and the test he set himself
chunks.text:
- He describes a chaotic year behind him: he left school, moved around (Airbnbs, country to country), with many ups and downs.
- He now feels stabilized: money in the bank, a home, a routine, a strong team, resources and the skill set. He calls it "the lottery ticket."
- The pressure that comes with it: with every piece in place, "there are no excuses" if he doesn't perform. He sees it as a test of whether he can execute, and says it is his duty to go all in.
- He is working on two things: his personal brand and a product called Study Buddy.

chunks.heading: Scaling the personal brand into a media company
chunks.text:
- The personal brand (YouTube, Twitter, Instagram) has become a real business, cash flowing over $40,000 a month.
- Plan: scale it and expand to new platforms and audiences, including:
  - Long-form YouTube (this video was his first long-form video, shot raw while walking down the street).
  - More short-form video.
  - A newsletter.
  - Possibly in-person events.
- Stated goal: turn "Oliver B", described as "a dude with a phone" on Twitter, into "a more legit media company."

chunks.heading: Study Buddy: what it is and where it stands
chunks.text:
- Study Buddy is an AI Chrome extension for students. A button is injected into an online assignment page (open-notes quizzes, homework). The student clicks it, the extension scrapes the question, runs it through AI, and returns the answer plus an explanation of why it's correct.
- Launched only a couple of months before the video. It scaled from zero to over 2,500 paid users.
- Current revenue: about $25,000 MRR. His goal is $250,000 MRR by end of year, which he calls "really, really possible."
- Ad spend to date: about $112,000 total, producing over $160,000 in revenue.

chunks.heading: The plateau: ad bans, no paid channels, and organic growth
chunks.text:
- Paid acquisition is blocked: Facebook is rejecting the ads, TikTok accounts are suspended, and Snapchat won't let them publish creatives. They have been unable to spend on marketing.
- MRR has sat at about $25k for 2-3 months. He says he's growth-oriented and gets frustrated and "exasperated" without visible upward movement.
- Despite that, the product grows 3-7% month over month organically, even with churn. His read: the product works, people love it, and they tell friends, so it has "huge legs."
- Work done during the plateau: many improvements to the landing page, the product and the user experience, with no change in the numbers.

chunks.heading: Testing acquisition channels and his mindset on the hard part
chunks.text:
- Current approach is to find channels that work, then pump spend behind them. Channels he's testing:
  - Meme pages.
  - Influencers at every size: micro, macro, and people with millions of followers.
  - TikTokers, Instagrammers and YouTubers.
  - Different paid ad platforms.
- His view on stage: "right now is literally the hardest part." Once something is working, it's easy to get to a 2, 5, 10, even 100 exit. At the moment nothing is working and there is no momentum.
- Metaphor he uses: the woodpecker hitting the tree. They've hit it about a hundred times and it only takes the 101st, 102nd or 103rd for it to crack. He says he can feel they are near the boiling point and that the key is patience.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Oliver Brocato explains how Tabs reached seven figures in year one with no paid ads. They designed a product that explains itself on camera, obsessed over launch details, then flooded TikTok, Reels and Shorts with content through creators on retainer running branded sub-accounts.

chunks.heading: Oliver's repost-everywhere growth system for a viral-by-design product
chunks.text:
- Before launching Tabs, Oliver and his cofounder Jake had a leggings drop-shipping brand that blew up on TikTok. The market saturated quickly as copycats came in.
- Their reset criteria were a product that can go viral and sell itself, and a product with high barriers to entry and a proprietary nature. Oliver says they agonized over branding, design, unboxing and the website before launch.
- Pay-per-click is "pretty linear": spend a set amount per purchase with little chance of exponential return. A cheap influencer post can pull a lot of views and sales.
- Oliver says the product is about 50% of the viral equation, and the creator the other 50%. Their influencers usually get more views on the paid Tabs post than on their normal organic content, which he uses as a pitch to creators.
- Tabs launched around December 20, 2021, with a few influencer posts and no big traction at first. About two weeks later Jake built the repost strategy.
- Result: Tabs grew without paid ads, with over 60 million views at the time of recording. Oliver says they do not run pay-per-click on Facebook, Google or Snapchat. Retargeting for abandoned carts and checkouts is the first paid move planned.

chunks.heading: Repost playbook: one TikTok, many platforms
chunks.text:
- Posts started as 2 posts per micro-influencer deal. They downloaded each video as an HD file without the watermark and reposted it on Instagram Reels, Facebook Reels, Spotlight and YouTube Shorts.
- The logo is removed because Oliver says platforms may restrict content that carries the TikTok logo. Natively uploaded reposts took off on brand-new accounts with no following.
- Virtual assistants posted hundreds of times a day. Oliver's logic: spam the platforms so one or two get picked up by the algorithm, then analyze what works and double down.
- This produced tens of millions of views on secondary repost accounts and meaningful revenue.
- Facebook Reels was an early win. One native Facebook Reel hit about 9 million views and drove a large number of sales in a day. Oliver says almost no brands post natively there.
- YouTube Shorts is the best short-form channel after TikTok. They run roughly 15 to 20 accounts, some pulling 10,000 to 20,000 views per video per day.
- Philosophy: "I can't tell you what video is going to go viral... but if I have 30 to 50 videos going live every single day and the quality is at least at a certain baseline, I know for sure that one will pop off." Oliver sums it up: "it's not about picking the needle in the haystack, it's about buying the whole haystack."

chunks.heading: Creator franchises: retainers plus subsidiary TikTok pages
chunks.text:
- Pain point: securing an influencer collab takes lots of effort and time. Oliver says nine out of ten influencers ghost you and keep the product even when you offer to pay on posting. It was very hard to scale at the velocity he wanted with VAs and interns managing it.
- Fix: put good creators on retainer to post on a recurring basis on their own pages. Then run subsidiary pages on TikTok, each managed by an independent creator.
- Searching "tabs chocolate" on TikTok shows about 25 brand pages. Operators include TikTokers, drop shippers, content creators, agencies, OnlyFans creators and college kids. Oliver says it does not matter who they are.
- Target: about 50 posts a day live on TikTok and about 50 a day across reposting platforms, "basically becoming a media conglomerate."
- Each creator gets a special link in their bio so Tabs can track sales impact. Top performers can become partners on a rev-share deal.
- Oliver frames them as "100% franchisees". Many are Shopify e-commerce operators who previously ran TikTok pages for their own brands and now take a share of Tabs as a content side hustle.
- Why it works (a point he agrees with): giving creators ownership of a Tabs page locks in the distribution channel better than asking for one-off posts. Oliver notes you cannot run multiple brand pages like this on Facebook.

chunks.heading: Double down when a video pops
chunks.text:
- When a video goes viral, they see it on the Shopify dashboard as a spike in visitors and sales, then text the team: where's the video, can we capitalize?
- Oliver says a follow-up video responding to a comment on the viral video, with a call to action, often outperforms the original despite getting about 1/10 to 1/20 of the views.
- When a creator or account pops, they start pumping more content on that account or have that influencer post more, to capture all the potential.
- Best single videos: a content creator's video with over 11 million views, and a micro-influencer in month one with 6.6 million views.

chunks.heading: Product and packaging engineered to make sense on camera
chunks.text:
- Oliver says Jake's idea was a clean diagonal break on each chocolate square. Each partner breaks it and takes half, so the concept is explained in about three seconds of video without paragraphs of copy.
- Positioning: sexual-enhancement products traditionally target men or women and stress discretion and no shame. Tabs flipped that into a fun, romantic product for you and your partner, any gender combination. Oliver says it differentiates them from competitors like Sex Crush on camera.
- The idea came from a competitor, Sextz, whose video had about 11 million TikTok views but whose packaging and execution were poor. Jake and Oliver copied the concept and executed it better.
- Details were deliberate: the shade of gold, the back of the box, and emojis revealed when you remove the chocolate. Oliver says there were many arguments over every detail.
- Build: contract manufacturer in Naples, Florida; boxes made in China; virgin polycarbonate molds and plastic wrappers; multiple supplement partners. It took about 11 months and many formulation iterations to pack in natural supplements without hurting taste. Oliver tested samples on friends around his fraternity house.
- Unboxing and packaging are essential to building for virality, since they put people in the right frame of mind.

chunks.heading: Site, conversion and AOV
chunks.text:
- Launch site was mobile only as an MVP, because traffic comes from TikTok, Snapchat and YouTube Shorts. Oliver says over 98% of traffic is mobile. A desktop site was in development at recording.
- They moved to pre-orders and stated transparently that delivery takes 4 to 12 weeks. Conversion rate dropped to about a third of what it had been. After catching up on pre-orders and removing the 4 to 12 week notice, conversion did not bounce back as he expected. They were reverse engineering why and A/B testing updates with the help of conversion rate optimization specialists.
- Pricing and AOV: a box (3 chocolates) sells for $30, with average order value in the mid $40s. They started with free shipping at 2 boxes to lift AOV.
- Test in progress: they removed the quantity selector because buyers mostly bought 1 or 2. It became a 1-box or 2-box option, defaulted to 2 boxes, with free shipping and a discount on the 2-box option to cut friction.

chunks.heading: Gifting lounge and where Tabs could go next
chunks.text:
- Oliver paid about $7,500 to sponsor a gifting suite lounge tied to a big event (Super Bowl, Met Gala or Oscars). They gave product to celebrities and could use photos at their discretion. He says most attendees were B and C listers and an A-lister would not come for free product.
- Wholesale: they were setting up a wholesale system after a few inbound requests, with TikTok still the main channel. The next product moves are flavors and box sizes (a 1-unit box for wholesale or retail, a 9-unit box).
- Oliver's category ideas: be "the sex shop for Gen Z" by destigmatizing a taboo category; functional foods that pair moods, flavors and supplements with common foods; and, when legal, THC, CBD and psilocybin edibles. He says the infrastructure would let them corner that market.
- He says they are not focused on the long-term vision yet. The priority is handling demand, production schedules and back-end logistics first.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Oliver Brocato explains how he built a viral-by-design product, then scaled organic TikTok with creators on retainer, one per account, plus a Discord affiliate army. He also covers the dropshipping-to-brand ladder, hiring lessons, and where organic stops working.

chunks.heading: Starting a chocolate-format brand: invent the product's format, not the formula
chunks.text:
- Tabs Chocolate sells "sex chocolate": three chocolate squares per box, each with a clean diagonal break so it splits into two triangles, one for him and one for his partner.
- Oliver says he did not reinvent the wheel or create a "crazy recipe". He took the most popular and effective natural supplements (normally pills and powders) and put them in a new format.
- The format is the differentiation. Pills and powders feel pharmaceutical and taboo, so competitors like Blue Chew and BYD advertise discreet packaging so "your girl won't even know".
- Tabs does the opposite: "embrace it with your partner, enjoy it with your partner, break it in half". Oliver says this also plays well on camera because the product explains itself visually.
- He and his partner picked the idea after a partner sent him a TikTok of a sex-chocolate product with about 8 million views and 2 million likes. The brand behind it had weak product and packaging, no social presence, no digital footprint and no ads. His reasoning was that a better-executed version could blow up.
- He designed the product to go viral on TikTok, and calls this "easy mode" compared with a random product.
- Results he cites for year one: over 250 million views across social, about $2.5 million in revenue, roughly 45% net profit margin, all organic. A recent month hit $500K in revenue, a record.

chunks.heading: Building the supply chain on a tiny budget
chunks.text:
- The first year went to building the product: supply chain, formulation, branding and packaging, before launching about a year before this interview.
- Tabs started with $30,000 total and was fully bootstrapped.
- Manufacturers would not talk to them. Minimum order quantities were typically 100,000 to 300,000 units.
- Oliver cold-called hundreds of companies until one agreed. That co-manufacturer works in micro runs, mostly by hand, and takes about three months per production run. Tabs later outgrew him.
- He lists the moving pieces: sourcing four or five supplements from separate manufacturers, the chocolate maker, the mold manufacturer, the boxes, and chrome polymer packaging that traps heat so the chocolate does not melt in transit.

chunks.heading: The TikTok organic system: one creator per brand page, volume as the strategy
chunks.text:
- His first approach was mass influencer outreach, and it was a headache at scale:
  - About 90% never respond.
  - Half of those who do charge exorbitant rates.
  - Of those who agree and get product, many ghost and keep it.
  - Outreach through VAs firing DMs hit Instagram action blocks, so he set up multiple accounts. He also used cold emails, texts and TikTok Creator Marketplace.
- His alternative was to hire creators to run brand pages, the way businesses hire a creator. He started with one creator on one page, then kept adding.
- Today he has 30 to 40 creators on retainer, posting one to three TikToks a day each.
- His reasoning on virality: TikTok's algorithm is a black box. He cannot predict which video will hit, but "if we put up 50 videos in a day, one will hit". Instead of finding the needle in the haystack, "grab the whole haystack".
- One creator per account, scaled horizontally across "subsidiary accounts". TikTok analyzes a page's creator style and content ethos to decide which audience to push to. Stacking several creators on one page confuses the algorithm ("too many cooks in the kitchen").
- Lesson: you do not need followers to hit the For You page; good content from a small account can still blow up.

chunks.heading: Affiliate Discord: 1,800 teens reposting viral content
chunks.text:
- Tabs runs a Discord with about 1,800 members, roughly 16 to 20 years old. Each gets a custom promo code that tracks the sales they drive.
- Each member makes their own subsidiary Instagram account and reposts Tabs' most viral videos to Instagram Reels, YouTube Shorts and Facebook Reels. Oliver says this collective has driven close to $500K.
- Oliver describes an affiliate as a "mercenary": an independent person with no relationship to the brand who captures a percentage of each sale they generate.
- Retention and growth tactics:
  - Invite competitions and daily bonuses.
  - Daily wheel spins where his VA enters names and the winner gets about $10, spun several times a day.
  - A community feel, including a gym chat where members post their physiques.
- He cites one 13-year-old in the Discord who made roughly $10-15K reposting videos, about 2 minutes a day.
- He is scaling the group and sees affiliates as a major lever.

chunks.heading: Paid ads limits and next growth levers for a restricted category
chunks.text:
- Because Tabs sits in the sex and supplement space, Facebook and TikTok restrict it. TikTok shadow-bans or deletes brand accounts, so he keeps coming back with new pages and new creators.
- He says this organic model probably cannot take Tabs to eight or nine figures. Brands without his restrictions, such as Mini Katana, can compound brand accounts into tens or hundreds of millions of views a month.
- He tried Trunk-style networks (unclear in the transcript) without success, and says he may not have given it a real shot.
- He says Tabs must crack paid media acquisition to move from a couple of million to tens of millions. Options he is exploring: creative advertising, landing pages, advertorials and cloaking.
- He notes comparisons with venture-backed brands are unfair: they can write off spend as brand awareness, while he needs a return on every dollar.
- Planned expansion:
  - Amazon, wholesale and retail (currently only small shops, sex shops and similar).
  - International, since over 40% of incoming traffic is international but they cannot sell there. Each country has its own supplement labeling and nutrition-facts rules.
- Ideas offered to him and one he is acting on: a lead-magnet product or ebook that can be advertised compliantly, such as a date idea book similar to The Adventure Challenge. He is building an ebook (a how-to guide) for email capture.
- He does not want expansion too fast: year one was a roller coaster.

chunks.heading: The entrepreneur ladder: dropshipping, private label, proprietary product
chunks.text:
- Oliver argues drop shippers are underappreciated and that dropshipping is arguably harder than running a brand. A brand banks on LTV and repeat customers and can be unprofitable on the front end. A drop shipper has to be profitable on the first purchase.
- His three-step ladder:
  - Dropshipping: no barriers to entry, costs $0, teaches skills.
  - Private label: find a product that works and put your logo on it (the leggings brand was his example).
  - A proprietary product: fewer competitors, higher barriers, a moat.
- He does not look down on the earlier rungs and sees them as fundamental steps.
- He criticizes brand builders who raise money without experience, burn cash, know nothing about performance marketing and outsource marketing, which he calls the hardest part of ecommerce. His line: "I'm a marketing company, I'm a media company."

chunks.heading: Career path: from fidget spinners to Tabs
chunks.text:
- At 14 he got a $500 loan from his grandfather, bought a 3D printer, a rubber mallet and skateboard bearings, and made fidget spinners in his basement. He sold to classmates, then recruited friends as sales reps, then went door to door to local shops, then moved to eBay and Etsy.
- He also grew a fidget-spinner Instagram account from zero to 10,000 followers using giveaways, hashtags, bots and follow/unfollow engagement tactics.
- When the trend died he tried dropshipping and failed, then started a social media management agency around age 15. His first client was his barber, who paid with a free haircut a month.
- He found Instagram management hard to attribute, so he moved into paid ads, where every dollar is measurable.
- In his senior year of high school he ran influencer collaborations for an app, "It's Me", spending $1,000 to $3,000 a day on micro influencers new to brand deals. The app reached number four in the social networking charts.
- He then ran TikTok and influencer marketing for a leggings brand that sold about $700K to $1M in a year. He says these were foundational even though they were not his own companies.
- Before Tabs he considered selling hot cocoa bombs, then switched to the sex-chocolate idea.

chunks.heading: Setbacks, mindset and where he points his energy
chunks.text:
- During the first summer, revenue fell about 60%. A co-founder disappeared for roughly three months, a summer intern tried to extort him for equity, and a roommate scammed him out of money. He was broke, moved back home with his parents and says his self-esteem collapsed.
- Hiring lesson: bring in specialists with defined roles and autonomy who know more than you in their domain, who should be teaching you, not generalists.
- Mindset points he states:
  - Success takes a long time, and Tabs would not exist without everything he did from age 14.
  - Early wins and losses are building blocks.
  - He had tied his identity to Tabs, then zoomed out. He loves the game and Tabs is a vehicle for it, but he does not plan to run it for 5-10 years.
- He runs a small social media agency on the side (six to eight brands at the time) applying the same systems: TikTok organic, Instagram, meme pages and Twitter memes.
- On Twitter, he uses his account as an unfiltered outlet and says it led him to investors, VCs, entrepreneurs and both of his roommates.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Oliver Brocato, a 21-year-old e-commerce founder, explains how years of small ventures led to TABS, a sexually enhancing chocolate built for TikTok that he scaled to about $11M a year. He covers sticking with one business through the early slump, focusing on the first customers, picking the right vehicle, and building a personal brand.

chunks.heading: Oliver's path into entrepreneurship and why he thinks ownership beats salary
chunks.text:
- Oliver started at 14 as a high-school freshman. He saw the fidget spinner trend explode in class, borrowed $500 from his grandpa, bought a 3D printer, manufactured the frames, hammered in skateboard bearings, and sold to friends, then local stores, then neighboring towns, then online on eBay and Etsy.
- He calls that first online sale his first taste of internet money: "people that didn't know me had zero connection to me... and they're giving me their money."
- From 14 to 18 he ran many projects: a social media management company that became a marketing agency, and running e-commerce operations for a friend's mom's fashion brand, taking it from about $300/day to $2,000/day in sales.
- His motivation: he grew up around much wealthier families (a friend's dad was a hedge fund manager) and saw his own dad, "a brilliant guy," earn through a corporate job. He concluded "the only way you really get rich is having ownership and equity, not getting paid per hour or per salary."
- Money was tight in his household and tied to constant pressure about SATs and the "right" school. Making money became validity nobody could argue with. He decided to "stop playing other people's games" and create his own path.
- Confidence compounds through a positive reinforcement cycle: a small business gets small wins, which leads to the next business, which attracts people who want to work with you.

chunks.heading: The rule against hustle porn: focus on the first customer, not the lifestyle
chunks.text:
- Oliver says the dream-and-consume trap is common. His point: talking about or watching content on building a business can feel like progress without producing any.
- He says to think "how do I get my first customer," not about the Lamborghini, the watch or the travel.
- The sequence he describes: get the first five customers, then the first 50, then the first 500, and let momentum "do the work for you."
- He says only people who actually do things build real confidence, while most people "only consume and consume."
- Surviving the early days takes an intrinsic drive or a "chip on your shoulder." He says "99% of people wash out" because early entrepreneurship is "eating [expletive] constantly."
- He says not to believe 99% of what you see online. His example: a Miami guy flexing a G-Wagon and a watch who, per a friend, couldn't use his apartment building's elevator because he had scammed other residents.

chunks.heading: Using TikTok early: influencer deals and the booty-lifting leggings
chunks.text:
- At 17 he was brought on by a friend (Alma man) to run influencer collaborations for an app on TikTok, when TikTok was still new.
- Why it worked: influencers had never monetized on the platform, so deals came "for pennies on the dollar," and users weren't yet bombarded with ads because other companies hadn't arrived.
- Result: a team of six took the app to number four on the social networking charts, right behind Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp.
- At 18 he teamed with a 17-year-old to push the viral TikTok booty-lifting leggings. They didn't create the product but were among the first to put it on TikTok.
- Path: started with dropshipping, then ordered inventory into the US, set up a 3PL, and private-labeled with their logo on the leggings.
- Outcome: zero to seven figures in about seven months.

chunks.heading: How Tabs was built: start with something already viral
chunks.text:
- Tabs is a sexually enhancing chocolate: popular natural supplements that usually come as pills or powder, put into a chocolate.
- His approach was the reverse of the usual order. Instead of making a product and figuring out marketing, he took something already viral with an "it factor" and built a business around a product that "lended itself well to TikTok." He says he created it for TikTok.
- Results he states: zero to eight figures, about $11 million in revenue this year, scaled from zero to $11M a year in two years.
- Tabs is being acquired. It cleared due diligence and the buyers sent the purchase agreement; he says it could still fall through.

chunks.heading: Learning by doing, pattern recognition, and the long game
chunks.text:
- He learns by experience, "trial and error and failing," not courses. Success is "the accumulation of tens of thousands of micro experiences" that build intuition through pattern recognition. He says there is no finish line, only the next level.
- Shiny object syndrome is "one of the biggest reasons" beginners fail online. His example: a friend who went crypto, then NFTs, then day trading, then dropshipping, then a TikTok content agency, switching every four months.
- He cites the "trough of sorrow" graph: initial honeymoon spike, then a drop as novelty wears off, then "false wiggles of hope," then eventually the promised land. He says his own sales chart "follows the trough of sorrow almost exactly."
- His rule: there are many ways to make money, so pick one, stick to it and see it through.
- On timing, he cites a tweet from the founder who sold Pura Vida for $120M: "it takes 10 years to do anything good." Skill compounds, and a few percent improvement every six months is a 3 to 10x difference over time.
- On juggling projects, he agrees multiple projects only work if they have synergies and feed each other.
- There's no single route to success: some people do 5am cold showers and journaling, while a "fat guy" who doesn't may hit the jackpot with a software business.

chunks.heading: Internet money, anonymous operators, and the founder's edge
chunks.text:
- He says skepticism of internet money is understandable because gurus flashing lifestyle and selling courses give it a bad rap.
- The biggest operators of e-commerce brands are often anonymous and look like normal people. Examples he says he knows personally: a friend selling slime in cups on track for over $20M, a friend selling mini katanas organically on TikTok on track for over $15M this year, and a 14-year-old making real money.
- Common thread among these people: they didn't fit the mainstream path, were "a little bit different," had hunger, and could take risk. "You kind of have to be a little bit crazy" to sell swords or slime online.
- His own edge, in his words: he's a marketer fascinated by consumer psychology. He looks at everyday businesses (an ice cream shop's table turnover, staffing) and thinks about optimization.
- Second edge: obsession. He thinks about his business 24/7, which he says can be a detriment but is his "competitive advantage," combined with being a quick learner who iterates constantly.

chunks.heading: What he does next: pick the vehicle carefully, build a personal brand
chunks.text:
- Current side projects: Study Buddy, a Chrome extension that runs online quiz or homework questions through AI and shows the answer plus an explanation. He launched it a few months ago and grew it from zero to $15,000 MRR despite summer, with no ads running. He plans to double down at the start of the school year.
- Personal brand: he is investing in content on Twitter, Instagram and short-form, with an editor, a content strategist and possibly a full-time camera person. He says he wants to be a business person first, so content comes from the business: "you don't want to create content, you want to be the content." He criticizes business YouTubers who have to brainstorm video ideas on a whiteboard.
- Why a personal brand: it gives "infinite reach," access to mentors and peers he could never meet otherwise, and luck "increases a hundredfold." Example: a three-hour lunch with an Israeli entrepreneur who sold a cybersecurity company to Microsoft for $200M. He says his brand makes him more money than his businesses.
- Next big venture: he wants to build a real team and infrastructure, maybe raise VC money, and "swing for the fences."
- Key lesson from Tabs: "the vehicle or the business that you choose is actually more important than your ability as an entrepreneur." An amazing entrepreneur with a bad product only goes so far, while an average one with the right product gets a rocket ship.
- He wants something he could do for 5 to 15 years or a lifetime, because that is what separates unicorns from companies worth millions or tens of millions.
- With his basic needs covered, he says he can "play the long game" and think in decades, which is hard when worried about the next lunch.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Oliver Brocato explains why he designed TABS around short-form virality instead of marketing an existing product. He covers scaling with many creator-run pages, moving to hybrid retainer plus revenue share, diversifying channels, using packaging for first purchase, and using a personal brand for hiring and networking.

chunks.heading: Marketing a product built for virality (TABS Chocolate)
chunks.text:
- Oliver describes TABS as an edible for sex: a high-end luxury chocolate, three squares per box, each square breaks in half to share with a partner. It packages popular natural supplements (usually pills or powders) into a less taboo, less pharmaceutical experience.
- He says he did not pick it out of love for the category: "it was a vehicle to go viral."
- His skill set was viral marketing on TikTok, so he built a product that could go viral by itself instead of marketing an existing one.
- Prior experience: at 18 he headed growth and partnerships for an app, took it to number four on the social networking charts behind Facebook and Instagram with a team of six, and was one of the people behind the viral TikTok Ripple woven booty-lifting leggings (no ownership in that company).
- Why it spreads: the product is visual and understandable in a 3-second clip or sound bite. A creator told him "even a monkey can make Tabs go viral."
- Influencers often get more views on sponsored TABS posts than on their own organic content. Oliver treats this as proof that product-first design for virality works.
- He argues short-form gives reach that would normally cost millions in paid advertising, and that TikTok has democratized virality: follower count matters little ("a thousand followers or a million").

chunks.heading: Why he moved from micro influencers to dedicated content creators
chunks.text:
- Starting plan: many micro influencers, because they give the best value per dollar. Bigger names cost more for brand name, managers and agencies charging 3x. The idea was to find undervalued creators, pay little, send free product.
- What failed: most influencers ghost; of those who reply, half charge ridiculous rates; some take free product and never post. Scaling was a logistics nightmare.
- He built a team of 8 scraping influencers, sent mass emails across 12 domains, and automated everything with Zapier (including an email triggered on chocolate delivery). He still could not crack it.
- Result: sales were a roller coaster, a good day after an influencer posted then back to zero. "That's not how you build a sustainable brand."
- Fix: hire one content creator to run a brand page called "tabs chocolate," be the face of it, and post 1-3 videos every day. In their first month the first creator generated about $70-80K in sales.
- Scaling: rather than adding creators to one page, he expanded horizontally, giving each creator an independent page. Hundreds of pages exist; many are inactive or dead because creators are hired and fired and accounts get shadowbanned, so new accounts are constantly created.
- He compares it to the Andrew Tate model: many people posting every day. He can't predict what hits, but with enough consistent volume from different people and pages, things go viral and drive revenue. He calls it a black box.

chunks.heading: Creator compensation: retainer plus upside
chunks.text:
- Pure affiliate sounds ideal but is hard to get people to accept at the start. Nobody wants to work for free, especially before a creator's content starts popping, which can take a couple of months.
- His model evolved: first creators on a retainer with renegotiation, then a hybrid. The hybrid is a very small retainer, "enough where they're happy if nothing happens", plus a percentage of all the upside.
- Result: creators making tens of thousands of dollars a month while driving hundreds of thousands a month for him.

chunks.heading: Diversify channels for longevity
chunks.text:
