- Oliver treats TikTok dependence as a real risk: pages get banned often and US government bans and hearings were in the news. His question: if TikTok goes away, does the business die?
- His answer: be "an octopus" with tentacles on 12 channels. Each channel growing incrementally (he cites 5%, 10%, 20%) compounds into a multi-million dollar brand.
- Use the 80/20 rule to find what drives most revenue and focus there, but build a durable company by doing everything well, not one thing.
- His current mix: email and text message ("crushing" them), a Google ads media buyer, Facebook ads he is starting to run himself, plus Instagram, Twitter and other creator work.

chunks.heading: Building a moat: lessons from the leggings business
chunks.text:
- The leggings brand was private label: they stuck their logo on someone else's product, ordered inventory and sold online. When it blew up, around 300 other people sold the same pair, the market saturated, and the business died as soon as it took off.
- Lesson: whatever he built next had to have high barriers to entry, be an amazing product that can't be ripped off, "own the industry, own the category," and be viral. He reverse-engineered the business from there.
- On execution, he says it is not genius: call the first 300 results when searching for chocolate co-manufacturers, find a box manufacturer on Alibaba. "It's not about IQ. Do you want it, are you hungry, and do you have enough experience and intuition."

chunks.heading: Packaging, product and repeat purchase
chunks.text:
- Packaging drives the first purchase. Customers can't touch or taste the chocolate online, so they judge by looks, like a first impression of a person.
- His test: put your product on a shelf against competitors; do eyes gravitate to it, or does it blend in with the herd?
- The product itself drives repeat purchase. If it isn't good, customers won't reorder just because the box was nice.
- A great product creates a flywheel: repeat orders, customers telling friends, friends talking about it.

chunks.heading: Personal brand as leverage
chunks.text:
- Oliver says he is a business guy first and a personal brand second. He compares content to sawdust: his business building is the saw, so he always has things to tweet and post about. He doesn't need to brainstorm ideas.
- Hiring: almost every hire on his team of 11+ people came from Twitter or a connection made through Twitter.
- Networking leverage: meeting that many people would take decades of networking events and flying around; content does it daily ("sitting on the toilet").
- He has no fixed goal for the personal brand, just the belief it is an asset that will likely be one of his most valuable and a lifelong one. Kids also message him that his content changed their perspective on college and business.

chunks.heading: Advice on building online
chunks.text:
- Do what you love instead of following conventional wisdom from parents and school. He says he knows "14-year-old degenerates" pulling half a million dollars a month online.
- He sees no barriers to entry: free education on YouTube, Twitter and social media if you follow the right people. Options he lists: create content, start a YouTube channel or TikTok page, build a brand or software.
- Expect slow results (maybe 5-10 years). If you stick with it and don't give up, "it's inevitable" you succeed.
- Context he gives on himself: he dropped out of the University of Michigan (Ross) last year to work on the business full time, and has been building brands and selling online since age 14.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Oliver Brocato explains how he picks products and channels that fit his edge, borrows proven ideas, and wins paid ads through a strong back-end (LTV, pricing, upsells) and heavy creative testing. He also covers channel-product fit, in-person distribution and super affiliates for his e-commerce brand-protection SaaS.

chunks.heading: Why Oliver moved from e-commerce into SaaS
chunks.text:
- Oliver sold Tabs (his chocolate e-commerce brand, scaled to $1M a month at age 21) and moved to software because he found it removed e-commerce's operational pain points.
- Inventory planning: he relied on viral traffic with month-over-month swings that were impossible to predict. In Tabs' first year the brand was out of stock and on pre-order for more time than it had inventory.
- Logistics: overseas and domestic manufacturers added moving parts, and "chocolate melts" over the summer.
- Iteration speed: improving a physical product means sample rounds with manufacturers, roughly a month each. A V2 or V3 can't ship until V1 inventory sells out, so a product change can take six months to a year.
- Software offers a shorter feedback loop, zero cost of goods, huge margins and "the only limit is your imagination."
- He says every part of a software business is measurable and can be tuned like a dial (onboarding, paywall, customer experience, accuracy, efficiency). Improving 3%, then 5%, then 8% ties directly to the P&L through lower churn, better retention and more revenue.
- He admits "the grass is always greener" and that each model trades one set of problems for another.

chunks.heading: How Oliver picks what to build
chunks.text:
- He leads as a marketer: "what has potential and opportunity to be pushed on TikTok or short form or paid ads," because that is his core competency and edge. He wouldn't start a construction company "because what the [ __ ] do I know about that."
- He lets others do the validation. If a mediocre product does $40,000 a month from a few YouTube videos, that is a signal that he can come in and make a dent. Seeing a competitor with your idea is "more signal," not a reason to quit.
- He frames innovation as micro-improvements: a buggy with a slightly better wheel, then a steam engine, and so on. Competition also creates an efficient market (a competitor can undercut on price and force others down).
- He doesn't believe in one-to-one copying. He takes inspiration piecemeal: one brand's website, another's email funnels, another's product packaging, and he studies the best constantly.
- Why pure copycats lose: the visible ad or page isn't what makes the money. The back end does: pricing split tests, email and SMS flows, and the ascension from subscriber to high-ticket customer. You can run the same ad as a competitor and lose money on it while they profit. He also warns that what a brand does today (for example Gymshark's flagship pop-up) isn't what got it there.
- His rule for a worrying competitor: a copycat that also does something a little better.

chunks.heading: Winning at paid ads: the machine behind the ad account
chunks.text:
- Oliver says he is not the best media buyer. His view is that winning ads is mostly about what sits behind the account, not only the media buying or creative.
- He cites a friend's mushroom gummy brand (name withheld). It has the same CAC as every competitor, but a fully optimized landing page and a layered upsell journey (cart upsells, a checkout popup offering two more bags for the price of one, more upsells in checkout) turn a $40 customer into a $100 customer. A higher LTV lets them afford a higher CAC than competitors.
- The product has to be really good too. If visitors churn after a week or a month, "you're kind of cooked from the start," regardless of ad quality.
- His LTV levers on his own SaaS:
  - Price testing: monthly billing amounts, trial offers, a free trial billed after a week or three days, and a $0.99 trial period then rebilling, which he found worked better than a free trial.
  - Paywall placement: paywall right away on the landing page versus after the user has used the product a bit.
  - Offer testing: "buy this and get a mystery gift," or "get this and also access to that." He calls these price tests that go beyond the dollar amount.
- He notes these elements all need to be dialed together: website, email and SMS, client ascension and ads.

chunks.heading: Creative testing and which metrics he watches
chunks.text:
- He ran Facebook ads himself, starting with help from Alex, a 17-year-old ecom and affiliate marketer who now does roughly $4M a month on his own stuff. Oliver later outsourced to a friend who runs a media buying agency, then switched to paying for a weekly audit call (about $250 for the call, roughly $1,000 a month, versus about $3,000 a month for the agency) to learn the skill himself.
- Lessons from those operators:
  - Scaling from six to seven figures a month "all comes down to creative testing and volume testing," plus split tests and A/B tests to find the winning angle.
  - Once there is a winning angle, remake it in variations: 10 different creators (a Black creator, a white creator, an older, a younger, a gay creator) remaking the same winning creative, or the same creative with different hooks.
  - Run each batch as a test, take the conclusions, then run a new batch and keep refining.
  - Pump spend into winning creatives; on Meta they can last a long time.
  - Give Meta time to spend and collect data, and don't touch the account constantly (his advisor recommended roughly once a week).
- Metrics: the only ones he really cares about are CAC and LTV. Hook rate (share who watch the first three seconds) and hold rate (how far they watch through) are correlated with performance, but he has had a creative with his best-ever hook and hold rates and a worse CAC than another creative. He doesn't think getting deep into the weeds is productive; if CAC and LTV balance, "you got a license to print money."
- On attribution, he relies on intuition trained by pattern recognition and looks at many data sources rather than any single tool or platform. At Tabs he could check sales at 10 a.m. and predict the day. He doesn't tell people to ignore data, and he doesn't rely on Hyros.
- He ran an incrementality-style test on one micro-SaaS: he scaled Facebook spend from $20k to $25k, $50k, $70k and $90k a month while Facebook still reported a steady CAC, yet overall revenue barely grew. When he later cut spend aggressively, MRR and revenue stayed the same. His takeaway: a lot of ad spend can be wasted, and platforms (whose incentive is for you to spend more) can't be fully trusted. Play "if I do this, what happens" games with spend.
- He hit about $180K MRR on one B2C micro-SaaS running ads (per Jaen's recollection of what Oliver said; Oliver didn't state the figure himself in this talk).

chunks.heading: Multi-creator organic strategy and channel testing
chunks.text:
- Oliver describes himself as the pioneer of the multi-creator strategy. The TikTok algorithm is "a bit of a lottery," so you want as many high-quality lottery tickets as possible.
- Setup: bring on many creators, each posting on their own independent account created from scratch by the creator, not a brand login and not tied to one device or email. Platforms see separate entities, each with its own chance to go viral.
- Results: at Tabs the creator program produced mid-six figures a month at its highest points. Content must be high quality ("not farmed from a YouTube video").
- It did not work for one of his consumer SaaS products. He used the same creators and principles; he tested seven or eight creators and none produced a viral video, a winner or a profitable result.
- His channel tests for his first micro-SaaS:
  - Organic multi-account creators: didn't work.
  - Instagram theme pages (which made six figures a month for his e-commerce brands): didn't work.
  - Google ads: not profitable.
  - TikTok ads: hit very hard.
- His lesson: the product or vehicle often determines which channel works, so "test a [ __ ] ton, fail a [ __ ] ton, and quickly" and move on. When you see a sliver of potential, "100x" it rather than just doubling down. Expect that 99% of what you try won't work.

chunks.heading: Bustm: why he chose e-commerce tooling and the go-to-market plan
chunks.text:
- Oliver's new B2B SaaS, Bustm, is "your digital watchdog" for e-commerce merchants. It scans social networks, marketplaces, Shopify sites and the wider web for copycats, infringers and counterfeits using a brand's IP (product images, whole landing pages, products, ads), then helps take them down.
- Takedown tools: one-click cease and desist letters (including physical mail), one-click DMCA notices, and automatic detection of the offender's providers and enablers (payment processor, email software, inventory software) so notices go to each. It also sends a letter to the owner's mom, to "name and shame."
- Why lawyers don't solve it: a lawsuit is expensive and slow, for "a couple dollars out of a 17-year-old dropshipper in a different country."
- Why he chose this market: he has an unfair advantage in e-commerce.
  - He has been in e-commerce since age 14 and knows many people in the industry.
  - He has about 45,000 e-commerce entrepreneurs following him on Twitter/X.
  - He has sent millions of dollars of deal flow and thousands of leads to about 14 agencies and software companies, which proves he can sell through his personal brand.
  - He believes he could sign 100 brands "tomorrow" through his contacts.
- Why not a course or an agency: a course has no equity, is short term and would burn relationships. An agency is "a glorified job" where the only way to scale is more human capital, and clients blame the agency when anything goes wrong. He wanted software he could sell to e-commerce merchants that makes their lives better. He says he didn't want to "sell people [ __ ]".
- Go-to-market plan (pre-revenue at the time):
  - Go to every e-commerce event and conference, shake hands and take people to dinner. He'll fly to big merchants to meet face to face. He says there will be no "rocket science content blitz."
  - Push through his own channels and recruit other e-commerce Twitter influencers.
  - Invest in SEO now, as a long-term bet.
  - Cold email and cold calls, testing everything and doubling down on what works.
  - Super affiliates: about 15 well-networked agency owners and software owners (people with a book of 10 to 50 merchant clients). One example is a former head of acquisition at an e-commerce software company with a rolodex of 500 brands doing $25M+ a year, who could send intros. Oliver says paying such a person something like $5,000 a month for intros could be the fastest ROI, or offer them advisorships or equity.
  - He finds super affiliates by DMing people, getting on calls, asking connected friends and attending conferences ("nothing we do is rocket science").

chunks.heading: Website conversion and compounding optimization
chunks.text:
- Oliver builds conversion-focused websites by studying e-commerce leaders instead of other B2B software sites. He names Javy Coffee (tens of millions a year, "probably one of the best optimized landing pages I've ever seen"), Carpe, Ora Nutrition and Seed as examples he takes notes from.
- He advises B2B founders to model their ads and websites on e-commerce players, whom he calls "the masters of conversion."
- He treats the website as never finished: pricing adjustments, banner changes, sticky cart and pricing card improvements, with a concerted effort each month to squeeze out small gains. His view is that 3% gains across every part of a business produce "a completely brand new business" in six months.
- He says things compound with time and he cites time as the most valuable asset, the same for everyone. His advice for the early stage is to first acquire a chunk of money and freedom, and ideally also build something you care about, since reinventing the wheel every month is exhausting.
- In-person distribution is "super underrated" for hitting your ICP: conferences pool thousands of ideal customers in one room, so "it's shooting fish in a barrel." He cautions against overcomplicating with too many channels.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Oliver Brocato explains moving from a viral consumer brand (Tabs) to B2B software (Bustm), including how he fixed pricing by switching to a performance model with a monitoring fee. He covers founder-led growth through his Twitter, word of mouth, and why a good product beats marketing machines in B2B.

chunks.heading: Oliver's path to Bustm and what the e-commerce years taught him
chunks.text:
- He started in e-commerce at 14 selling fidget spinners. Along the way he did Instagram meme-page ad deals, a social media management business that became a marketing agency, influencer management for an app that raised $10 million in VC funding, and a drop-shipping store selling booty-lifting leggings.
- At 19 he started Tabs, a "viral sex chocolate": the most popular natural supplements, normally pills or powders, in a new format. He made a stigmatized, taboo category feel "very sexy and romantic."
- Tabs got billions of views on TikTok, Instagram and other channels, scaled to eight figures a year, and exited for "a nice cash out" around age 21-22.
- After Tabs he ran a ChatGPT-wrapper Chrome extension. It scaled nicely, but he wasn't passionate about it and couldn't see doing it long term.
- He started Bustm.com in January of the year before this interview (2024 or 2025, depending on timing; the source doesn't say which) and had 100+ brands by November 2025.
- He picked it because it solves a pain he lived with at Tabs. He calls it "productled growth" and "something that I wish that I had when I was running my business."

chunks.heading: How Bustm works
chunks.text:
- Bustm is software plus a team of IP specialists and enforcement agents. It finds copycats and counterfeits that rip off e-commerce brands, then gets them taken down.
- **Detection:** the software scrapes a brand's images and keywords, runs thousands of searches, crawls the results and surfaces one-to-one matches, scanning every day.
- **Enforcement:** the team reports bad actors to the platform, the domain registrar and the payment processor, without spending "six figures and 3 years in court."
- **Why this works:** the bad guy won't stop if asked. The enablers are legitimate US companies (Stripe, Shopify, Amazon) that must act or risk being negligent and exposed to lawsuits or class actions. So Bustm goes after the enablers and goes "back and forth until we get them removed."
- **Approval step:** brands must approve each flagged target before enforcement, so Bustm doesn't accidentally report a competitor, supplier, whitelisted creator or authorized reseller.
- It's currently "half software half agency." The goal is to automate everything with AI agents.
- Brand-side harms he cites: duped websites, copied Meta ads, clones bidding on the brand's keywords, fake marketplace listings, stolen Amazon buy box, counterfeit or never-shipped products, and customers who get scammed and never buy from that brand again.
- One client's CPM dropped about 50% and Meta spent more on their creative after Bustm took down a bad actor bidding on the same keywords.
- Some takedowns have turned into clients: former drop shippers came back saying they now build real brands and get trademarks.

chunks.heading: Pricing: from retainer to performance plus monitoring fee
chunks.text:
- **Original model:** unlimited monitoring and takedowns for $2,000-$5,000 a month, by brand size and infringer volume.
- **Problem:** at $3-5K a month, brands were very sensitive to results. Bustm only finds and reports; platforms decide whether to act, and they can be slow. Without strong wins, brands wanted to churn. This was worst early, before strong team, processes and SOPs. He says effectiveness is now "three or 4x" higher.
- **Per-kill idea:** he modeled it from one month of actual data (about $50-60K revenue from 20-25 retainers) to price per-takedown at $50-$200 so revenue would match. He first pitched it as a downsell when prospects balked at the retainer.
- **Result:** everyone said yes. He went from closing a couple of brands a month to one or more a day.
- **Problem:** with $0 to start, brands signed but never approved targets, so no takedowns happened. Roughly twice as many brands were on performance deals as retainers, and Bustm earned nothing from them.
- **Fix:** a call with every brand to add a monthly monitoring fee "just to cover our cost and bases." Most were receptive. Some left, which he welcomed as it weeded out tire kickers.
- **Current model:** $300 a month monitoring plus $50-$200 per takedown, alongside the $2-5K unlimited tier.
- **Lesson:** "If you're willing to pay something then you'll be willing to take stuff down."
- **Retention signal:** September had only about $3,000 in churn, which he calls "basically like zero churn."

chunks.heading: B2B distribution: founder brand, referrals and product quality
chunks.text:
- Tabs ran on scaled creator and paid distribution: hundreds to thousands of creators posting daily, an army of 7,000 clippers, and sometimes hundreds of thousands of dollars a month on meme pages on Instagram and Twitter.
- For Bustm, he says clipping and creators don't work, and ads are tough to crack.
- Bustm grows from his personal brand, about 50,000 e-commerce entrepreneurs following him on X, plus word of mouth and referrals. "I am my marketing." His content covers his journey, case studies and success stories, such as saving brands hundreds of thousands or even millions of dollars by removing copycats.
- Inbound is now 3-5 booked calls a day from referrals, "found you through Oliver," or word of mouth, with no marketing spend.
- On B2B vs consumer: in e-commerce it's about ad creative and distribution; in B2B "how good is your [ __ ]" is the biggest growth hack, because e-com founders are friends and talk. A weak product means "a churn and burn operation."
- He prefers a business that can survive and grow on word of mouth over one where you "dump a dollar in to get a $1.20 out" and fight CPM increases and shifting market conditions. He says that kind of business compounds.
- Growth plans:
  - Hire a full-time ghostwriter who shadows him, joins meetings and produces content (not an agency or one tweet a day).
  - Cites Adam Robinson (retention.com, RB2B), who he says went from zero to $6 million ARR bootstrapped through LinkedIn and founder content.
  - Starting to test paid ads and other channels, and building a sales team (his first sales hire was brand new at the time).
- His principle: double down on what works.

chunks.heading: Selling B2B: long cycles and early-stage suffering
chunks.text:
- Consumer Tabs sold at $29.99 to Gen Z impulse buyers off a TikTok video. B2B means higher price points, multiple stakeholders, finance and legal sign-off, and sales cycles of three weeks to multiple months.
- It is "hand-to-hand combat on every sale": emails, texts, calls, no-shows and reschedules.
- He took 600-700 sales calls himself in about eight months, and says it was humbling to go from running a multi-million-dollar brand to getting no-showed.
- He says every business has to "be bad first." Nobody starts with packaging, pricing and fulfillment dialed in, so B2B has an infancy stage you have to fight through.
- He rates value delivered as separate from product features: improving the customer experience can mean giving clients more perceived value, not only a better product. The same product made clients unhappy at $3K retainers and happy on performance pricing.
- Priorities: more wins, more bad guys found, more successful takedowns, and a better customer experience.

chunks.heading: Surviving failures at Tabs and in a new category
chunks.text:
- He compares the journey to the S&P chart: daily or weekly views look like a yo-yo, but the long-term view is a line of best fit up and to the right. "It's never as deep as the way that it feels."
- **Tabs stockout in COVID:** inventory sold out fast, but containers were stuck off the coast and the packaging was made in China, so restocking took about six months. Spending on marketing or ads made no sense, and pre-orders were running while momentum died.
- Restarting took three or four months to get back to a similar level. He expected to turn marketing back on and "be rippy again," and it didn't work that way. He had left college as a sophomore to run Tabs.
- Other Tabs problems:
  - Chocolates melt in summer.
  - Disputes with his business partner.
  - The sale nearly fell through multiple times, with about $50,000 in legal fees and four months running a process.
  - Affiliate fraud: affiliates bought with stolen credit cards, got paid commission, then chargebacks hit, costing $5-10K a day at one point.
  - His best creators and his right-hand person quit.
- At Bustm, selling a business and starting over means rebuilding the foundation of team and momentum, which "takes years to build."
- Operating mindset: he has tried to be less anxious. He says CEOs should create urgency, but constant fight-or-flight is unhealthy for him and the team. He wants seasons of pushing and seasons of coasting.
- He says he's having far more fun running Bustm with compounding growth and happy clients than he did with Tabs' blitz scaling, where "every month we reset from zero."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Oliver Brocato walks through building Tabs (physical product), Study Buddy (consumer software) and BustM (software-enabled agency). He argues for learning attention and distribution, copying validated ideas, charging from day one, and fixing operations and hiring before pushing growth.

chunks.heading: Choosing a niche and building the right skill first
chunks.text:
- Oliver says that to make money online, the answer may be less a business model than a skill set you think you're better at than most people, in something you enjoy.
- His argument: building a business takes heavy sacrifice and hard work. If you hate what you do, you compete against people who "love it" and "live and breathe it," and you probably fail.
- He says you can "literally make money doing anything." His examples: people who made millions in Roblox and Minecraft, and a Minecraft skins and maps seller doing over $1M/month. Oliver's own first business was Minecraft and it made his first million.
- He calls the social media boom one of the biggest opportunities of his generation. Pick an interest (cars, cooking, knitting), make short-form video about it, build a following, then work out how to monetize.
- He thinks younger people (10 to 30) have an edge because older, more experienced people don't understand social dynamics.
- Every young person he knows who is "absolutely killing it" is doing something around social media.
- His advice for the very first dollar is counterintuitive for a founder: go work for or apprentice under someone a few steps ahead of you. He calls this "probably the biggest shortcut."
- The core skill he wants people to learn is getting impressions, views and clicks through social media. If you can't afford to hire people for it, you have to learn it yourself.
- He notes that many of the best online businesses have an internal creator or content team, or the founder does the content.

chunks.heading: Distribution is the biggest lever in every business model
chunks.text:
- Oliver's view: attention and distribution are the lever across ecom, consumer software, B2B software and info.
- Ecom: "that's like the biggest lever that separates winners and losers in ecom is your ad creative" (Meta ads). He allows this is an oversimplification given product and website matter.
- Consumer software: same thing, ad creative.
- B2B software: "the biggest cheat code of B2B software is a founder personal brand."
- His proof: with about 50,000 X followers, he changed his link in bio to a 30-minute consulting call. He charged $300, then $500, then about $1,250, and did over 100 calls in a year to a year and a half without promoting it.
- His B2B software business went from zero to $370K MRR in under a year and a half, mostly off his personal brand and Twitter following.
- He stopped the consulting calls because they were boring (everyone asked how to go viral on TikTok) and because he agrees you don't get rich selling your time. He prefers building assets with enterprise value, though he says truly passive businesses are mostly a myth.
- His working method: get eyeballs first, then work backwards to the best way to monetize them.

chunks.heading: Learning from early exposure and local role models
chunks.text:
- Oliver saw it was possible through a high school senior who sold 3D-printed fidget spinners and advertised on meme pages (stories and 24-hour shoutouts), reaching hundreds of thousands of dollars a month at peak.
- He also followed the big ecom gurus of the time, but says the local example was what made it feel real.
- He started his own fidget spinner company, listing early on eBay and Etsy and ranking well organically by being early.
- He helped a friend's mom scale her boutique fashion brand, then worked for that senior, who mentored him. He acted as a VA on an app growth project that raised $10M, handling creators, negotiating and overseeing posts.
- Earnings were small, but the payoff was exposure, pattern recognition and intuition, so when he started his own businesses he wasn't "scratching and trying to figure everything out."
- His point: joining someone else's tribe shortcuts a lot of pain. Going alone from the start is "way, way too overwhelming."

chunks.heading: Picking a product: validate it, then execute better
chunks.text:
- On Tabs (an aphrodisiac chocolate brand he took past $10M a year from age 19 to about 21), the lessons from earlier ecom were that logo-slapped products got saturated, ad returns compressed and margins dropped. So he wanted something novel and hard to copy.
- Tabs was a food and supplement product. It took over a year from idea to launch, and he says that in the make-money-online world a year is like ten for others.
- Virality was designed in: each chocolate square breaks in half, one half per partner, so a TikTok can show how it works without a word.
- Validation came from a competitor's TikTok with about 7M views and 2M likes. That competitor had no social presence, no ads and barely a website, which Oliver calls a "dumpster fire of execution." He brought ecom experience and improved the product.
- Cost: about $30,000 total to get a first production run worth about $100,000 retail, which sold out in the first three weeks.
- His rule: don't try to invent something wholly new. Do something with existing validation, then tweak, iterate and improve. Nvidia made chips for video games; Slash (a bank for internet businesses) started with sneaker resellers.
- On a client's competitor: a prospect already working with a competitor "means they have a problem" and a budget. He argues they may be better clients, and he challenged his COO's plan to avoid them.
- Moats: food products are hard because of co-manufacturers, formulation R&D and minimum order quantities. But "the biggest moat comes down to the execution." His example is Cal AI (photo calorie tracker), which went from $0 to $30M a year despite about 400 clones, because it executes better on ads, onboarding conversion and pricing, which lets it afford a higher acquisition cost.
- With AI builders, Shopify and tools like Cursor and Claude, building is cheap, so "strong operators will win."

chunks.heading: Study Buddy: a single painpoint and a scaling playbook
chunks.text:
- Study Buddy is a Chrome extension where you screenshot a problem, AI answers and gives step-by-step solutions.
- His principle: find a very specific micro niche, solve one pain point very well, and have an "aha moment." Don't build "the everything app."
- It didn't need to be novel. It removed friction students already had (copy, open a tab, paste into ChatGPT, or text a friend).
- First attempt: he ran the Tabs playbook (creators, influencers, meme pages). He sank about $10 to 20K and got back only a couple thousand dollars.
- What worked: testing channels until TikTok ads, using his best organic videos as the ads.
- Back-end optimization: he changed pricing from $20/month to $5/week, added a trial and tested a 99 cent trial.
- Retention was strong. He turned ads off in the summer (acquisition cost roughly doubled out of school year) and the app still kept growing from word of mouth.
- Numbers: TikTok ads gave about $35 to $40 LTV against about a $7 CAC. Meta ads gave about a $20 CAC against about a $55 LTV.

chunks.heading: Bust: the MVP, free pilots, and charging early
chunks.text:
- Bust (BustM) scans the internet for ecom brands and finds copycats, counterfeits and unauthorized resellers, then gets them removed. It targets their infrastructure (domain, registrar, host, payment processor) with complaints and evidence, with about a 70% success rate. Brands pay a monthly subscription.
- Timeline: idea in September 2024. He found a technical co-founder via Y Combinator's co-founder matching (no YC needed). The co-founder flew to Miami, slept on his couch and built the MVP in about 48 hours. Oliver gave him a sizable chunk of the business.
- Launch: he teased "a crazy AI tool for ecom brands" to his Instagram and Twitter audience and sought beta testers doing over $1M a month. He stayed secretive on what it was, and his DMs flooded.
- He gave 20 to 30 brands free access and says he regrets it. They didn't even log in, the Slack was "ghost and crickets," and the feedback wasn't honest.
- His rule: people who pay give real feedback. His first $5,000/month client "was on our asses" and produced more insight than all the free users combined.
- He disputes that you should work for free, even for agencies: a real price earns respect, and free "discredits you." If you can't charge, you aren't providing enough value. At most, give a discounted rate.
- Charging started in February 2025, about four weeks after beta began. March 1 revenue was about $30 to 35K MRR, and the second month about $80 to 85K MRR, a run rate near $1M a year.
- The software MVP made brands do hours of takedown "homework," which they refused, so he pivoted it into a service. He hired a virtual assistant from South Africa, ran a shared Slack channel and a Google spreadsheet, and did everything manually end to end. Brands paid for that.

chunks.heading: Fixing fulfillment and hiring to scale Bust past $80K to about $375K MRR
chunks.text:
- Around spring 2025, revenue sat near $80K and then dipped. Clients churned because results were poor (they paid about $3K a month). Takedown success was about 20%, the team was reporting to wrong inboxes and resubmitting the same evidence.
- Team at that point: Oliver, one engineer and one VA. Oliver did all marketing, growth and sales, and the engineer was acting as a pseudo account manager in Slack.
- Fixes, in order:
  - He paused growth and gave clients a free month. He went from one VA to about four.
  - He pulled the engineer out of Slack and said the only job was writing code.
  - He hired an operations lead (a former chief of staff at another ecom software company) to own day-to-day delivery.
  - He hired Tony from a competitor to train the VAs. With SOPs and processes, success rose from 20% to 40, 60, 70 and then about 80%.
- He then went back to selling and took 600 to 700 sales calls himself.
- He replaced the first engineer, who was building a fully automated pipeline that would take years. The new engineer shipped easy wins (small automations in a day) and a client dashboard instead of spreadsheets. Oliver paid the first engineer out with six figures.
- The hire went in when revenue was about $30K a month with about $10K profit, against a $12 to 15K a month salary. It cost a negative month (around June), and since then revenue has grown every month. He says he was hiring "players," not stars: "get asses in seats."
- Current team: about 40 people, including a three-person dev team, an ops head, a client success manager, a head of brand protection with 10 years of experience, about 25 South African VAs, multiple sales people, and a pod focused on the first 30 days of new clients and at-risk accounts.
- Targets: about $375K to nearly $400K MRR now, with the aim of a million a month. He is learning org charts, company values, OKRs and a weekly CEO dashboard with department heads.

chunks.heading: Growth is trial and error, and where Oliver is focused now
chunks.text:
- Acquisition channels so far: his Twitter following (about 40 calls a month, a ceiling he hasn't broken), cold email (about 15 calls a month; a cold email agency took volume from 100K to 600K emails a month and quality and bookings fell), and Meta ads (about 20 calls a month, near break-even; cost per call went from about $560 to $1,200, which he attributes to ad fatigue or macro shifts).
- He is now pulling back Meta, running dinners and events, and hired a head of partnerships to cross-sell and share leads with companies that serve ecom brands.
- He cites Hormozi: "one acquisition channel, one avatar, one offer until you get to a million a month," and admits founders often chase a new channel instead of confronting the skill gap behind a plateau. He thinks the answer is probably going deeper in one channel.
- His view: "growth is expensive and growth is very hard" because most things you test won't hit, and testing needs real budget, time and effort.
- He read Alex Becker's tweet on the Hyros funnel (5 sales call webinar versions, 25+ ads, over $100K in ad tests, 153 audiences, 22 landing page variations, 200+ hours). His takeaway: top operators make it look effortless, but "none of this is easy" and there is no silver bullet.
- Current priorities: a new pricing model (rolled out), a better sales hire, content aimed at bigger "enterprisey" brands (a better writer), an appointment setter, engineers, a client success manager and a lead brand protection specialist.
- Churn is about 6 to 8% monthly, per the host's mention, and Oliver acknowledges it could be better.
- Team lessons: ecom brands can be very lean (Primal Queen, a 100M-plus brand with three co-founders; Melo Sleep, zero to $100M in about eight months). Bust is the opposite: a human-capital business where "you're only as good as your team."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Oliver Brocato explains how counterfeits and copycats nearly bankrupted his chocolate brand, then how he built Bustem to fight them. Bustem is a hybrid of AI automation and human analysts sold as a roughly $3k/month retainer. He covers productizing a services business, free audits as the sales motion, and who should and shouldn't buy.

chunks.heading: Oliver's path into e-commerce
chunks.text:
- Oliver started at 14 selling fidget spinners online. He was one of the first to list them on eBay and Etsy.
- He moved into drop shipping, including booty-lifting leggings that blew up on TikTok.
- He then started Tabs Chocolate, an aphrodisiac chocolate that splits in half so each partner gets a half.
- He scaled Tabs from 0 to 11 million a year, dropped out of college, and sold the business.
- Counterfeits, copycats and unauthorized resellers "almost bankrupted the company multiple times." That pain point led him to build Bustem after the exit.

chunks.heading: The universal truth about scaling an e-commerce brand
chunks.text:
- Oliver's rule: "if you're in e-commerce and you start making money, people start trying to rip your [stuff]."
- The threats he saw:
  - TikTok Shop sellers.
  - Chinese sellers on Temu, Alibaba and Shein.
  - Resellers on eBay, Walmart, Etsy and Amazon stealing the buy box.
  - Drop shippers and black hat operators who clone a site one-to-one and bid on the brand keyword, hijacking branded search traffic.
- He found his first dupe when his mom texted him an ad for one. He describes it as butterflies, fight or flight, and a knot in the stomach.
- Visible copycats are "the tip of the iceberg." If a founder sees a couple, Oliver says he can almost guarantee there are many more and that revenue is being lost.

chunks.heading: Why small copycats still hurt: death by a thousand paper cuts
chunks.text:
- One junk listing alone won't dent a business. Spread across Amazon, TikTok Shop, Temu, Walmart, eBay, Etsy and standalone sites, together they become "a parasite" that drains energy, dollars and resources.
- Some Bustem clients are hit by thousands of bad actors a month. It is "whack-a-mole": take five down and three pop back up.
- Revenue loss is only one cost:
  - Brand reputation is ruined when fakes get shipped or never shipped at all, which brings bad reviews.
  - Fake supplements can be dangerous.
- Example he cites: AG1 pulled its product off Amazon because so many dupes appeared. It then spent a year or two working with Amazon lawyers and authorities before relisting recently. Oliver's point is the opportunity cost of letting the problem get out of hand: "you don't want to be the next AG1."
- Some competitors began as rippers. They copy your images, ads and website, make money, then invest in their own photos, site and ads. Taking no action gives them runway and money to become full competitors, "and by the time that happens, you have no recourse."
- Analogy he uses: "Would you let people walk into your warehouse, take products out and just walk right out?" Copycats do the same thing virtually.
- Bad actors behave like bullies. If you create enough friction and stand up to them, they move on to an easier target.

chunks.heading: Why lawyers and cease-and-desist letters are the wrong first tool
chunks.text:
- Positioning: Bustem is not a law firm and not licensed lawyers. Oliver calls it "the cheaper sister or cousin of the law firm" and "the first line of defense" before paying someone $500 or $1,000 an hour.
- A cease and desist "will get thrown out" by bad actors.
- Litigation takes years and can cost hundreds of thousands of dollars, and the defendant can declare bankruptcy, leaving you "holding the bag."
- Using a bazooka on one small seller is wasteful. It makes sense only if someone is stealing millions. For 300 small infringers you can't file 300 lawsuits.
- Many in-house general counsels and law firms work with Bustem. They hand off the "bottom of the barrel" volume work and focus on the high-leverage cases.
- Oliver is clear it is not a silver bullet. The target is a 70 to 80% removal rate, and he says the rest can go to a lawyer.

chunks.heading: The enforcement approach: attack the infrastructure, not the bad guy
chunks.text:
- Sending a letter to the bad actor himself gets thrown out.
- Bustem goes after the infrastructure that supports the bad actor: the domain, the registrar, the hosting provider, the payment processor and the platform.
- Reasoning: those parties are white hat players who don't want to be liable or "holding the bag." Bustem shows them proof that the customer is a bad actor and says that continuing to support them creates liability for them too.
- About 80% of enforcement is automated. AI agents fill out abuse forms and report inboxes at registrars, hosts, payment processors and platforms.
- Bustem also gets sites delisted from Google and flagged so visitors see a warning that the site isn't authorized.
- Reported success rate: 70 to 80% of targets crippled or removed from the internet.

chunks.heading: How Bustem's detection works, end to end
chunks.text:
1. Onboarding: the brand fills out questions, uploads documents, and signs a power of attorney so Bustem can enforce on its behalf. It connects Shopify, social accounts and Amazon storefront.
2. Asset bank: Bustem scrapes the brand's images, keywords, product titles and brand search terms.
3. Daily searches: thousands of searches a day across platforms and social channels. These include reverse image search, frame-by-frame breakdown of videos, product titles, brand names and keyword combinations.
4. AI triage: each search returns a huge number of results. AI analysis and cross-image comparison find the one-to-one matches among them.
5. Human review: a team of 30+ identification analysts manually reviews what the AI and automation surface.
6. Client approval: the brand clicks "bust them" to approve or denies each one. Denials ask for a reason, such as not interested or an authorized reseller that goes on the whitelist. Approvals and denials feed machine learning and train the analysts to surface more relevant results.
7. Enforcement: after approval, Bustem works the takedown via the infrastructure route above.
8. The scan reruns every day, so it keeps surfacing net-new and repeat infringers who pop back up.

chunks.heading: The hybrid software plus human service model
chunks.text:
- Oliver describes the product as hybrid: AI agents and automation plus a human team of identification analysts, enforcement agents, a team lead, a client success manager and a head of brand protection.
- Every client gets its own Slack channel. Oliver's insight: clients don't want to log into a platform or have homework. They "just want these bad guys taken down."
- Weekly automations post into the Slack channel: what was found, actions taken, removals, and the economic value regained. Bustem calculates how much revenue the removed bad actors were doing.
- This delivers "white glove agency" service on a productized, efficient backend, which is how Oliver says it works at scale and cost-effectively.
- Pricing: about 170 brands as clients, including Comfort Clothing, Oats Overnight, Primal Queen and Neurogum. The average retainer is about $3,000 a month. Oliver says a hit team, expert software and everything else for that price is very affordable, and that he may eventually take a percentage of the economic value recovered.

chunks.heading: Who should buy, and how to sell it
chunks.text:
- Fit: Oliver says a brand should be doing more than $100,000 a month. Below that, "you got bigger problems to worry about." He says to get back "in the ad account" and scale rather than invest in trademarks early. Elsewhere in the interview he says Bustem works with brands doing more than a million a year that see some sort of problem.
- Sales motion: lead with value, not a sales call. A prospect books a 20 to 30 minute call. Before the call, Bustem runs a full 360-degree threat scan across social platforms, marketplaces and the wider internet.
- On the call it walks through the findings, the removal plan and the process. The audit is free and the prospect keeps it whether or not they hire Bustem. If the problem isn't bad enough, Oliver says Bustem will tell them to come back when it is.
- Customers' own counter-ads act as proof of demand. Brands like Santa Cruz Medicinals and Underbrush run ads telling customers not to be scammed by fakes. Oliver says seeing those is "fuel and reassurance" that he is solving a real problem.
- Counterfeit ads often run aggressively at the bottom of the funnel, so a hypers-scaling copycat can capture a brand's hot traffic and force a brand to descale. Oliver's view: counterfeiters are parasites that suck dollars out of an advertiser's account.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: An essay by Bustem's founder on how to tell original brands from copycats and what to do when you're copied: audit your IP, register trademarks, differentiate on customer focus, confront professionally, and out-innovate imitators. Argues copycats compete on features while authentic brands build on emotional connection, loyalty and speed.

chunks.heading: How Oliver defines and spots a copycat brand
chunks.text:
- Oliver defines a copycat brand as one that imitates another business's products, services, or overall identity to profit from its reputation without original ideas or innovation.
- He separates copycats from counterfeits. A copycat gets as close as possible to a well-known brand (shape, packaging, colour, name) without clearly infringing, while a counterfeit is a fake product.
- He lists the signs of a copycat brand:
  - Follows rather than leads, so it lacks originality.
  - Lacks focus and tries to cater to everyone with a sprawl of products and services.
  - Messaging is generic, talks about features, and shows no empathy for a defined audience.
  - Built on a service-based Unique Selling Proposition instead of the customer's emotional state.
  - Single-use offers with no customer journey, so it has to keep chasing new customers.
  - Forgettable: looks, sounds, and acts like everyone else offering the same thing.
- His example scenario is a skateboard gear seller who finds a social page with their products, an almost identical logo and name, and a bargain-hunter audience instead of the premium one they built.

chunks.heading: Why copycats are dangerous
chunks.text:
- They erode trust: buyers expect the original's quality, and if disappointed, the real brand takes the reputational hit, not the copycat.
- They take sales and dilute market share and profitability.
- They create consumer risk. A lookalike electronic device may not meet safety standards.
- They often infringe trademarks, which forces the original brand to divert resources from innovation to defending its IP.
- AI makes this worse. He points to deepfake endorsements, AI-generated fake reviews (the FTC's Impersonation Rule from April 2024 and its August 2024 rule banning fake reviews and testimonials), and WIPO guidance on generative AI and IP risk.

chunks.heading: What makes a brand authentic, and what copycats can't copy
chunks.text:
- Authentic brands are built on a unique value proposition, innovative products, and a distinct voice, which builds loyalty and brand equity.
- They know exactly who they serve, keep things simple, and close the loop by collecting customer feedback.
- Oliver says original brands build on the "Unique Buying State of the Customer", not on features. He cites that about 65% of purchasing decisions are emotional, so their messaging targets the customer's emotional state before and after purchase.
- Feature-based positioning is short-term, because competitors catch up and force constant reinvention.
- Authentic brands design for the customer's stage in the sales cycle. They offer minimal, much cheaper entry offers so prospects can taste the brand before committing a large sum.
- Copycats can't easily replicate:
  - Customer relationships and trust built over years.
  - Organizational culture and accumulated expertise.
  - Brand story and values.
  - The innovation pipeline.

chunks.heading: Legal frame: passing off, confusion, and unfair advantage
chunks.text:
- He frames most copycat cases around two grounds: likelihood of confusion, and unfair advantage or detriment to a mark's distinctive character or reputation.
- Quote he uses from Perry v Truefitt: "A man is not to sell his own goods under the pretence that they are the goods of another man."
- The more distinctive the mark (Kodak, Zappos, Apple), the easier it is to prove confusion. Generic or descriptive marks make confusion harder to establish.
- Cases he cites:
  - Reckitt & Colman v Borden (1990), the "Jif Lemon" case that set the passing-off test.
  - United Biscuits v Asda (1997), Puffin vs Penguin biscuits, where similar packaging misled consumers.
  - Red Bull v Big Horn (2020): no confusion was found, but the copycat still took unfair advantage of the branding.
  - Thatchers v Aldi: Aldi's "Taurus Cloudy Cider Lemon" did not infringe, because the names were aurally and conceptually different.
  - William Grant & Sons v Lidl: the court found it hard to see the Hampstead gin redesign as coincidental, giving Hendrick's a reasonable prospect on intent.
- Unfair advantage can be found even without intent to exploit the reputation.

chunks.heading: Five ways Oliver says to deal with copycats
chunks.text:
**1. Be flattered, then run an IP audit.**
- Reframe the anger: being copied signals the business is successful enough to imitate.
- Before calling an attorney, check trademark, copyright, trade dress, and patent exposure.
- Document consumer confusion, and screenshot and archive evidence with timestamps.
- For minor, clear infringement, a well-crafted cease and desist often resolves it cheaply. If the copying is extensive, intentional, and causing measurable harm, hire an IP attorney.

**2. Mark your territory with IP protection before it's needed.**
- Register trademarks for name, logo, taglines, and distinctive product names, including variations.
- Register copyright for your most valuable assets (site content, product photography, marketing videos, training materials), because registration unlocks statutory damages and attorney's fees.
- Keep dated records of asset creation, product launches, and market entry.
- Fight when the copying hits revenue, causes confusion, is in your core markets, involves your registered marks, or when you must enforce consistently to keep strong rights.
- Monitor but don't engage when the similarity is superficial, the market or geography is different, enforcement would cost more than the damage, or only unprotectable ideas are copied.
- Use platform tools such as Amazon Brand Registry and Project Zero, the TikTok IP Protection Center, and AI monitoring plus DMCA takedown services, since swift action can resolve things in days rather than months.

**3. Differentiate and stay customer-focused.**
- He quotes Bezos: "If we can keep our competitors focused on us while we stay focused on the customer, ultimately we'll turn out all right."
- Time spent obsessing over imitators instead of customers erodes the advantage.
- Invest in deep customer understanding, superior service delivery, and continuous value creation. Customers with good experiences become less price-sensitive.
- He notes a copycat watching you is neglecting its own strategy, which tends to lead to mediocrity.

**4. Confront the copycat directly and professionally.**
- Reach out before involving lawyers: it can reveal their motives, resolve things faster, and preserve relationships.
- Be professional, not personal. Ask questions first, state specific concerns, explain the business impact, and offer solutions such as changing branding or messaging.
- It works best with small operators, no sign of malice, recent copying, and a willingness to find an acceptable outcome.
- Skip straight to a cease and desist or DMCA notice when the copying is intentional, informal contact was ignored, registered marks or copyrights are involved, confusion is already happening, they operate at scale, or they copy multiple competitors.
- Document all communications either way.

**5. Out-innovate them.**
- He calls innovation the ultimate defense: by the time a copycat replicates today's offering, you've moved to the next generation, which makes copying less economically viable.
- Tactics: adopt emerging tech first, foster experimentation, fund R&D even when business is good, and stay close to evolving customer needs.
- He adds strategic partnerships, patents and trademarks for key breakthroughs, and co-innovation with engaged customers who then resist switching to imitations.
- Operational quality (reliability, delivery speed, support) counts as innovation and is more defensible than product features, because it's embedded in the organization.
- Innovation compounds, so the gap to imitators widens over time.

chunks.heading: Oliver's background and what Bustem does
chunks.text:
- Oliver is the founder of Bustem. Before it, he built, scaled, and exited an 8-figure e-commerce brand and experienced knockoffs, copycats, and counterfeits firsthand.
- He says Bustem has enforced takedowns on more than 100,000 listings, reclaimed over $1M in lost revenue, and protected 120+ brands.
- Its customers include 7-, 8-, and 9-figure e-commerce brands, with Comfrt, Plunge, and Mellow Sleep named.
- Bustem scans for unauthorized use of a store's images, videos, headlines, and text, and streamlines takedowns with pre-filled DMCA forms and case management. It offers free scans, 24/7 monitoring, and bulk takedowns.
- His pitch figures: more than 2M DMCA notices filed daily, and businesses losing $29B a year to content theft.
- He times the message to Q4, urging brands not to let copycats eat their BFCM revenue.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Bustem founder Oliver Brocato explains how e-commerce brands can defend against counterfeits. Register your IP first, enforce takedowns on platforms rather than litigate, monitor at scale because infringers keep reappearing, tighten the supply chain, and educate customers.

chunks.heading: Why counterfeits and IP theft hurt a brand
chunks.text:
Oliver, who built, scaled, and exited an 8-figure e-commerce brand before founding Bustem, treats counterfeits as a direct hit to reputation, not just lost sales. His framing:

- A counterfeit uses someone else's trademark without permission so the maker profits from the owner's reputation.
- Shoppers who meet fakes can lose trust in the genuine product, even when the brand had no control over the situation.
- Fakes are usually inferior, which drives bad reviews on third-party sites from customers who received fakes instead of originals.
- Unauthorized sellers eat into margins and sales through price gouging and heavy discounting. This frustrates retail partners and can sever those relationships.
- Shoppers hunt for low prices, so they get tricked into buying a near-identical fake in place of the real item.

chunks.heading: Growth of the problem (figures he cites)
chunks.text:
- 26% of shoppers saw a rise in counterfeits during the pandemic (Intelligence Node survey).
- US CBP seized 26,503 shipments in 2020 containing IP-violating goods, estimated at nearly $1.3 billion had they been genuine.
- 38% of surveyed shoppers came across counterfeit essential items online during the pandemic.
- Shopper distrust by marketplace: eBay (80%) and Amazon (53%) got the most votes for selling counterfeits; one in four shoppers said they stopped buying from eBay.
- Most-counterfeited luxury brands: Louis Vuitton (56%) and Gucci (52%).
- Bustem's own claim: businesses lose $29B annually to content theft, and over 2M DMCA notices are filed daily.

chunks.heading: The four types of IP and how each gets violated
chunks.text:
Oliver lists what a business can own:
- **Patents:** the right to exclude others from making, using, selling, or importing the invention. Design patents cover ornamental appearance; utility patents cover function. In the EU they usually last 20 years.
- **Trademarks:** any word, phrase, symbol, design, or combination that identifies your goods and distinguishes you from competitors (Nike symbol, Apple logo). One trademark can cover a range of products, unlike a patent.
- **Copyrights:** protect original works (writing, photos, video, software code, art). Protection is automatic, but he recommends registering if you plan to sell or enforce.
- **Trade secrets:** formulas, methods, and processes you keep secret for economic value. The holder must proactively protect them.

Common violations: patent infringement, trademark use or deliberate lookalike marks, copyright theft of written work, photos, and video, and selling counterfeit products (which can hit patent, copyright, and trademark at once).

His principle on detection: the best defense is being mindful of violations yourself. The sooner you detect and stop one, the better your chance of protecting profits, goodwill, and market position.

chunks.heading: Step one: register your IP
chunks.text:
- Registering IP is "the most elementary step" because it lets you prove you own it when you find fakes.
- IP generally must be registered in each country under national law, since copyrights, patents, and trademarks are not globally valid. Registering at home lets you start protecting the brand internationally.

chunks.heading: Choosing an enforcement strategy: litigation vs. takedowns
chunks.text:
- Decide your goal first, then pick the strategy.
- Litigation can produce court orders to stop infringement, monetary damages, disgorged profits, and lawyer's fees. You must prove the fake listings misled customers and hurt your brand.
- He calls it a poor fit when the goal is fast removal of listings and protecting reputation and sales: it is time-consuming, expensive, and has no guarantee of success. Consider it only after weighing risks and rewards.
- His default is enforcing against the listings directly. The first step is taking them down, and the process depends on the platform. E-commerce platforms and social networks generally know the problem and support enforcement, so knowing each platform's process lets you act fast.

chunks.heading: Takedowns are whack-a-mole, so monitor and enforce at scale
chunks.text:
- Taking down one counterfeit does not solve the problem. Infringers re-list across multiple marketplaces and countries, so individual enforcement hits its limit.
- His answer is scanning the internet continuously and submitting takedowns at scale with technology, monitoring and enforcing internationally across marketplaces.
- Bustem's approach (his product): automatically scan billions of websites for unauthorized use of store content, videos, headlines, and text. Then streamline takedowns with pre-filled DMCA forms and case management, 24/7 monitoring, instant detection, and bulk takedowns.
- Stated results: enforced takedowns on 100,000+ listings, reclaimed over $1M in lost revenue, and protected 120+ brands.

chunks.heading: Supply chain and anti-counterfeiting technology
chunks.text:
- **Supply chain:** counterfeiters exploit loopholes. Use strong supplier contracts and maintain traceability.
- **Physical authentication tools he lists:** holograms and security labels, unique serial numbers and barcodes (traceability and recalls), RFID tags with encrypted data, and tamper-evident packaging.
- **Track and trace:** barcodes, RFID, and GPS to follow products through the supply chain, detect diversion, and find where counterfeiting happens.
- **Authentication apps:** consumers scan a QR code or barcode to verify origin and manufacturing details.
- **Online monitoring and enforcement:** watch marketplaces, social channels, and ecommerce sites for fake or unauthorized listings, using software to automate detection and takedown.

chunks.heading: Collaboration and customer education
chunks.text:
- Work with law enforcement and industry associations to share intelligence, coordinate enforcement, and support legal action. Build those relationships before you need them.
- Educate customers: tell them where to buy legitimate products, list unauthorized products on the market and how to spot them, and explain how to report suspected fakes.
- Encourage customer reviews, since shoppers rely on reviews and ratings when deciding what to buy.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A founder-written checklist for protecting a brand from counterfeits and copycats: register IP and domains, monitor continuously, enforce fast, use AI detection, and revisit the plan regularly. It is partly a content piece for Bustem, so the value is in the practical sequence of protect, monitor, enforce and iterate.

chunks.heading: How Oliver defines brand protection and why he cares
chunks.text:
- Oliver founded Bustem, a copycat detection and takedown tool for e-commerce merchants. Before that he built, scaled and exited an 8-figure e-commerce brand, where he "experienced firsthand the pain of knockoffs, copycats, and counterfeits."
- Bustem's stated results: takedowns on 100,000+ listings, over $1M in lost revenue reclaimed, 120+ brands protected, from startups to global enterprises. It is trusted by 200+ 7, 8 and 9-figure e-com brands, including Comfrt, Plunge and Mellow Sleep.
- He defines brand protection as proactively safeguarding a company's intellectual property, reputation and other assets, to prevent misuse, counterfeiting or reputational harm.
- The stakes he cites: counterfeiting is 2.5% of global trade (OECD), and businesses lose $29B annually to content theft. Counterfeits confuse customers and hurt a legitimate brand's trust, not just its revenue.
- His reputation-crisis example: if a trusted snack brand reported a contamination issue, customers would panic and abandon it even if the product was safe, and recovery of reputation and sales would be slow. Protection means safeguarding the brand before, during and after a crisis.
- A copycat copying your product images or descriptions hurts you three ways: it diverts traffic and sales, it can outrank your original content in search, and it confuses customers and dilutes the unique value of your products.

chunks.heading: The legal and domain foundation
chunks.text:
- **Trademarks:** register your brand name, logo and distinctive elements so you have exclusive rights to use them in the marketplace.
- **Patents:** if you create new products or processes, patent them to block competitors from replicating them.
- **Copyrights:** register written content, software and digital media. Registration gives you the legal grounds to act against infringers.
- **Domains:** register your brand domain as soon as you create the brand, before a counterfeiter does. Consider brand-aligned TLDs (.com, .net, .org, niche TLDs).
- **Typosquatting:** monitor domains that use common misspellings of your name. They cost you traffic and trust and enable phishing and customer confusion.

chunks.heading: Build recognition and monitor continuously
chunks.text:
- Consistent logo, colors and fonts across all packaging, marketing and online platforms strengthen recognition and deter imitators.
- Write brand guidelines for your team, partners and third-party vendors so the brand is represented uniformly.
- He says to build protection in from the beginning, as you build the brand, and to keep the brand management team on the same page.
- Registering trademarks and domains is not the end. He calls for continuous monitoring so you catch infringement before it harms you:
  - Trademark monitoring: check trademark databases and scan marketplaces like Amazon and eBay for counterfeits.
  - Social media monitoring: use social listening to track brand mentions and unauthorized use, since counterfeit goods and copycat products are often advertised there.
  - Search engine monitoring: watch results for counterfeit websites or fraudulent sellers using your name.
  - Tools he names: Google Alerts and Brandwatch.
- A strong online presence, he argues, connects you with customers and makes it harder for counterfeiters to trick them. He cites an OECD finding that brands prioritizing online presence handle infringement better, with less revenue loss. He gives Nike as an example of a brand fighting fake sites and social accounts.

chunks.heading: The enforcement ladder when infringement happens
chunks.text:
- He expects infringement to occur despite your best efforts, so act "quickly and decisively." The escalation order:
  1. **Cease and desist letter:** often the first step. A formal notice asking the infringer to stop using your brand assets.
  2. **Legal action:** if it continues or escalates, file a lawsuit or seek an injunction, which can stop the infringement and win damages.
  3. **Online enforcement:** use platform takedown channels at Amazon, eBay, Google and similar.
- Bustem's own approach to takedowns: pre-filled DMCA forms, case management, 24/7 monitoring, instant detection and bulk takedowns. He notes over 2M DMCA notices are filed daily.
- When vetting a provider, he says to check that it has automated takedowns and can enforce on difficult social channels such as Telegram, has established relationships with relevant authorities, and has the right patents and experience for your needs.

chunks.heading: Technology, experts and combining old with new
chunks.text:
- Use AI and automated tools to scan the internet for counterfeits and trademark infringements. You can do it manually, "but why waste time" when tools can, leaving you to focus on legal action and strategy.
- Going DIY is hard: it needs constant checking and infringements slip through the cracks. Many businesses hire a specialized brand protection or DMCA takedown agency.
- What agencies offer, in his view: monitoring, enforcement and legal support; knowledge of IP law; relationships with major platforms and regulators; global coverage across countries with different laws; and time savings through automation.
- Mix old and new: offline methods like customs checks and border protection stop fakes entering the market, while online tools fight cyber threats. OCR (optical character recognition) can find fake goods that don't show up in ordinary searches.
- Where the field is heading in 2025 and beyond:
  - AI-driven visual detection, real-time monitoring and cross-platform enforcement.
  - 31.8% of shoppers first discovered fake goods on social media (State of Brand Protection Report 2025), so every channel needs guarding.
  - Deep learning on images: a study reached 99.71% accuracy telling genuine from fake garments from smartphone photos. Brands no longer need to rely on keyword monitoring alone, since fakes can be flagged even when titles and copy are disguised.
  - Closer partnership with marketplaces, such as Amazon embedding AI in its brand protection tools.

chunks.heading: Internal alignment and consumer education
chunks.text:
- Educate every key department about brand protection: sales, marketing, digital, legal, manufacturing, supply chain and finance. Teach them to recognize brand abuse, report it, and apply the protection strategies.
- Educate consumers too: show them how to identify genuine products and the harm of fakes by sharing unique product features, price guidelines and security indicators.

chunks.heading: Setting up a protection program
chunks.text:
1. **Assess brand risks.** List threats (cyber-attacks, social media scandals, negative reviews), analyze each one's impact on finances and customer trust, and estimate likelihood and frequency from past incidents and trends. He warns small issues can escalate into major crises if ignored.
2. **Write a protection plan.** Set clear objectives, identify threats such as counterfeiting and trademark infringement and decide the action for each, and allocate budget for monitoring software, legal counsel and employee training. Define roles, protocols and a clear escalation path for internal reporting and for communicating with affected customers and partners.
3. **Engage a provider.** Research services, patents and experience, match offerings to your needs, and confirm partnerships with authorities, automated takedowns and hard-channel enforcement.
4. **Monitor and update.** Track incidents reported, response times and resolutions achieved, stay current on industry trends and emerging risks, and refine the strategy from new insights and stakeholder feedback. He says you can't "set it and forget it."

chunks.heading: Advanced stage: when infringers keep coming back
chunks.text:
- The signal for moving up: you face a high volume of counterfeits and repeat infringers.
- His advanced playbook:
  - Connect the dots to find the source of the problem.
  - Shift into business intelligence gathering mode.
  - Integrate online and offline protection efforts.
  - Take a proactive approach to IP infringement.
- He says the right insights to inform decisions are what separate a regular strategy from an outstanding one.
